#939. Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

#938. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bernd Leno (Fulham): Unbelievable couple of saves from him to keep Fulham in the game. I thought Newcastle should have been three or four up before Fulham got the equaliser.

Ronald Araujo (Liverpool): He is just the difference maker to that Liverpool backline. The injury-time Crystal Palace penalty that denied them a clean sheet was a terrible decision, but when he is in the team, they play better and look more solid.

Jair Cunha (Nottingham Forest): Exceptional. His goal helps, but exceptional at sniffing out the danger. Erling Haaland didn't have a sniff of a goal in Man City's defeat by Forest. Cunha will need to be really good going forward if they're the team Oliver Glasner wants.

Tarik Muharemovic (Leeds United): Many times he got caught one v one against Spurs but showed his ability to be chilled and calm under pressure and make his tackle. Very unassuming.

Nordi Mukiele (Sunderland): He was excellent again. He forced Chelsea to go wide and I think that was the key to them winning the game.

Leon Goretzka (Aston Villa): Although it was 4-4 in the end at Man Utd, Goretzka was a beast. He was calm under pressure and moved the ball really well as well. He obviously got a goal but his passing, movement and the ability to just be calm and handle every situation presented to him was really, really good.

Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool): How this guy has not got a new deal I don't know. He keeps coming up big, high energy and he is vitally important to the way Liverpool play. When he is fit and available and firing on all cylinders it feels like they have a chance in this title race.

Enzo Le Fee (Sunderland): Where would Sunderland be without this guy? He has been good, he has been scoring, chipping in with big moments. Also his ability to take the ball when under pressure, take his side up the pitch and also have that little bit of innovative play and free thinking. He is exceptional.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (Everton): Bossed the game for Everton against Coventry. Unbelievable goal but he absolutely bossed it. There was nothing more he could have done. Never gave the ball away, defensively he was solid. Attacking wise - goals and assists.

Thierno Barry (Everton): The two up front pick themselves, but probably the last time I would have them together in the same team. Did really well, two good goals against Coventry and probably should have had a third as well.

Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest): What a game for him and moment he needed. A lot of pressure from the outside, including myself. Hasn't shown up big this season but against his former team Man City, his former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca as well, and he turned around and said, 'you know what, I am the man and you should have kept me around'. Scored two unbelievable goals, led the line well and looked physically fitter and stronger. Maybe now that confidence comes through and we see the best of him after the international break.

Mikel Arteta (Arsenal): I am going for Mikel Arteta simply because he has just won the Premier League. Well done. I said at the start of the season that, for me, Arsenal will win the league by 10 points and this weekend they did it. It's November and the season is officially over.

#935. Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared

The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

Key ins: Bruno Guimarães (Newcastle, £75m), Ezri Konsa (Aston Villa, £51m), Piero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m)

Key outs: Leandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m), Gabriel Jesus (Barcelona, £8.6m), Fábio Vieira (Hamburg, £7.7m), Christian Nørgaard (Everton, £7m), Ethan Nwaneri (Borussia Dortmund, loan)

It is all change at Villa and, although a little trepidation is inevitable, a refresh was probably overdue. At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. Last summer there was concern Villa had gone stale and 12 months ago they ended up fretting on deadline day – Harvey Elliott and Jadon Sancho joined on loan – but there was no such chaos this time. Ben Fisher

Key ins: Johan Manzambi (Freiburg, £51m), Nicolas Jackson (Chelsea, £47.5m), Ibrahim Mbaye (PSG, £47m), João Gomes (Wolves, £34m), Zion Suzuki (Parma, £30m), Taylor Harwood-Bellis (Southampton, £25m), Matteo Ruggeri (Atlético Madrid, £21.4m), Leon Goretzka (Bayern Munich, free), Aaron Wan-Bissaka (West Ham, loan), Alejandro Garnacho (Chelsea, loan)

Key outs: Morgan Rogers (Chelsea, £117m), Ollie Watkins (Al-Hilal, £51m), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal, £51m), Youri Tielemans (Manchester United, £35m), Donyell Malen (Roma, £21.6m), Lewis Dobbin (Southampton, £9m), Lucas Digne (PSG, £8.5m), Emiliano Martínez (Chelsea, £7.5m), Evann Guessand (Crystal Palace, loan)

The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?

Perhaps Bournemouth’s best business was keeping hold of their coveted key players, chiefly Eli Junior Kroupi, Rayan, Alex Scott and Tyler Adams. Bournemouth rejected bids from Chelsea for Scott and stayed true to their plan of resisting offers to give Marco Rose the best chance of succeeding, with the club attempting to juggle European competition and the league for the first time. The arrival of the Portugal centre-back António Silva, 22, from Benfica looks a typically smart replacement for Marcos Senesi, 29. Kroupi’s freak foot injury, which will probably keep him out until November, may have proved a blessing in disguise in terms of retaining the 20-year-old. BF

Key ins: António Silva (Benfica, £21.4m), Álvaro Rodríguez (Elche, £21.3m), Juanlu Sánchez (Sevilla, £11.1m), Michele Di Gregorio (Juventus, loan)

Key outs: Luis Sinisterra (Cruzeiro, £5.2m), Enes Unal (Getafe, free), Álex Jiménez (Fiorentina, loan), Marcos Senesi (Tottenham, free)

Avoiding a repeat of last year’s upheaval was a major boost. Keith Andrews held on to his best players and made smart additions to a solid squad. Mamadou Sangaré has added quality in midfield since joining from Lens and looks the bargain of the summer. Callum Wilson has brought experience up front after signing on a free and Jaidon Anthony provides cover on the flanks after his £15m move from Burnley. El Hadji-Malick Diouf, signed from West Ham, offers potential at left-back. Jacob Steinberg

Key ins: Mamadou Sangaré (Lens, £39m), El Hadji Malick Diouf (West Ham, £35m), Jaidon Anthony (Burnley, £15m), Jannik Schuster (Red Bull Salzburg, £14m), Callum Wilson (West Ham, free)

Key outs: Ethan Pinnock (Coventry, £6m), Jordan Henderson (Chelsea, free)

Deadline day deals to bring in the exciting Nigeria forward Femi Azeez from Millwall and the Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés from Stuttgart made it 12 signings in another summer of transition, Azeez’s arrival being announced almost 12 hours after the window shut. The departures of Jan Paul van Hecke, Carlos Baleba and Carl Rushworth brought in more than £140m as the Brighton model continues to deliver big profits, although losing last season’s top scorer, Danny Welbeck, to Chelsea for a mere £5m may be the biggest loss if the new striker Promise David cannot bring the goals. EA

Key ins: Luka Vuskovic (Tottenham, £46m), Zadok Yohanna (AIK, £21.5m), Chema Andrés (Stuttgart, £18.9m), Pascal Struijk (Leeds, £18m), Femi Azeez (Millwall, £15m), Jaouen Hadjam (Young Boys, £11.1m), Costinha (Olympiakos, £11m), Michael Svoboda (Venezia, £4.3m), Promise David (Union St-Gilloise, loan)

Key outs: Carlos Baleba (Manchester United, £70m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham, £52m), Carl Rushworth (Coventry, £22.5m), Diego Coppola (Paris FC, £15.3m), Danny Welbeck (Chelsea, £5m), Joël Veltman (West Ham, free), James Milner (retired), Solly March (released)

Xabi Alonso’s appointment as manager was the biggest signing of the summer. Chelsea have been sensible since turning to the Spaniard. Morgan Rogers has started well after joining for £117m. Maxence Lacroix adds power in defence, Marco Palestra versatility on the flanks. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson can raise standards in the dressing room. But there was the usual revolving door. Money was made on a host of outgoings. Marc Cucurella, one of the world’s best left-backs and sold to Real Madrid, looks a bigger loss than Enzo Fernández. However a worry is that Chelsea did not replace Fernández after selling him to Manchester City for £125m, their late £47m move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara collapsing at the last. JS

Key ins: Morgan Rogers (Aston Villa, £117m), Maxence Lacroix (Crystal Palace, £52m), Marco Palestra (Atalanta, £47m), Geovany Quenda (Sporting, £40m), Valentín Barco (Strasbourg, £34m), Emmanuel Emegha (Strasbourg, £21.6m), Pep Chavarría (Rayo Vallecano, £16.3m), Emiliano Martínez (Aston Villa, £7.5m), Danny Welbeck (Brighton, £5m), Jordan Henderson (Brentford, free)

Key outs: Enzo Fernández (Manchester City, £125m), Marc Cucurella (Real Madrid, £52m), Andrey Santos (Manchester United, £50m), Nicolas Jackson (Aston Villa, £47.5m), Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest, £45m), Trevoh Chalobah (Como 1907, £25.7m), Tyrique George (Everton, £18m), Marc Guiu (RB Leipzig, £14.5m), Tosin Adarabioyo (Tottenham, £7m), Axel Disasi (Crystal Palace, loan), Alejandro Garnacho (Aston Villa, loan), Benoît Badiashile (Napoli, loan), Robert Sánchez (Como, loan), Mykhailo Mudryk (Tottenham, loan)

It remains to be seen whether Coventry have struck the right balance in the market. Frank Lampard wanted to maintain momentum but add power and physicality. Coventry also sought to address their lack of Premier League experience with Taiwo Awoniyi and Ethan Pinnock. Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers last season but the step up means the pressure is on Awoniyi, never prolific for Nottingham Forest, Sidiki Cherif, a promising 19-year-old, and Ellis Simms to deliver before Haji Wright returns from injury. Stephen Mfuni, a teenage loanee from Manchester City and their 11th and final summer signing, increases their left-back options. BF

Key ins: Caleb Yirenkyi (Nordsjælland, £23m), Carl Rushworth (Brighton, £22.5m), Sidiki Cherif (Fenerbahce, £20.5m), Loum Tchaouna (Burnley, £20m), Aurèle Amenda (Eintracht Frankfurt, £15.4m), Taiwo Awoniyi (Nottingham Forest, £9m), Ethan Pinnock (Brentford, £6m), Gustavo Hamer (Sheffield United, £6m), Stephen Mfuni (Manchester City, loan), Frank Onyeka (Brentford, undisclosed), Dan Bentley (Wolves, undisclosed)

The lost tug of war with Sunderland over Malick Fofana summed up another chaotic deadline day for Palace, who were still scrambling for signings in the final minutes and confirmed the arrivals of Ben Chilwell, Quinten Timber and Darío Osorio after the window shut. The new manager, Pierre Sage, will at least be pleased to have secured more defensive reinforcements after losing Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea, with the loanees Honest Ahanor and Axel Disasi adding much-needed depth. Palace also kept hold of Ismaïla Sarr – presuming he doesn’t join a club in Saudi Arabia before the Sunday deadline there – after rejecting an approach from Liverpool for the Senegal forward. EA

Key ins: Anan Khalaili (Union St-Gilloise, £21m), Quinten Timber (Marseille, £15m), Zavier Gozo (Real Salt Lake, £11m), Axel Disasi (Chelsea, loan), Evann Guessand (Aston Villa, loan), Honest Ahanor (Atalanta, loan), Darío Osorio (Midtjylland, loan), Dwight McNeil (Everton, swap), Takehiro Tomiyasu (Ajax, free), Óscar Mingueza (Celta Vigo, free), Ben Chilwell (Strasbourg, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Maxence Lacroix (Chelsea, £52m), Daniel Muñoz (Nottingham Forest, £22m), Brennan Johnson (Everton, swap), Borna Sosa (Cologne, loan)

It was a window that revealed the extent of The Friedkin Group’s ambitions, the strength of the club’s finances after the move to a new stadium, the state of the relationship between the manager and chief executive and the expertise of the senior leadership team; and none of it was positive. The owners deserve some credit for listening to fans and halting the self-defeating sale of Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest but otherwise it was a modest window that descended into a shambles. The club’s best player was sold for a below-market fee, a move for Folarin Balogun collapsed and although the equally desperate search for a right-back ended with Ainsley Maitland-Niles signing, David Moyes was left with one striker and a smaller squad than he started the day with, despite repeatedly urging his employers to strengthen. AH

Key ins: Tyrique George (Chelsea, £18m), Merlin Röhl (Freiburg, £17.3m), Hayden Hackney (Middlesbrough, £16.5m), Christian Nørgaard (Arsenal, £7m), Ainsley Maitland-Niles (Lyon, £4.3m), Brennan Johnson (Crystal Palace, swap), Jack Grealish (Manchester City, loan)

Key outs: Iliman Ndiaye (Manchester City, £60m), Beto (Fiorentina, £15.4m), Tim Iroegbunam (Hull, £13m), Dwight McNeil (Crystal Palace, swap), Idrissa Gueye (Al-Diriyah, free), Nathan Patterson (Torino, free), Séamus Coleman (released)

It was a summer of change at Craven Cottage. Marco Silva departed after five successful years in charge and was replaced by the inexperienced Álvaro Arbeloa, who has focused on adding youth. Gonzalo García, César Palacios and Manuel Ángel followed Arbeloa from Real Madrid and Shea Charles is an exciting signing from Southampton. Some stalwarts have left. Raúl Jiménez joined Wolves and Harry Wilson went to Leeds. Fulham looked to strengthen. They secured the midfielder Hugo Larsson and centre-back David Affengruber on deadline day but missed out on another target, the right-back Andrei Ratiu. JS

Key outs: Sasa Lukic (Ipswich, £9m), Issa Diop (Ipswich, £8.5m), Harry Wilson (Leeds, free), Raúl Jiménez (Wolves, free)

“Think of us like a volcano,” said Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, in early July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Two months on the Ilicali has presided over 18 signings, investing more than £150m and his manager, Sergej Jakirovic, has choreographed two Premier League wins. The horizon looks infinitely brighter than in June, when the playoff winners sold two players for a combined £8.5m to avoid breaching English Football League spending rules and a near-certain six-point deduction. Hull, remember, spent last season under a two-window EFL transfer embargo. They have compensated for that this summer and, although time will tell whether all those new faces are compatible, reasons for optimism remain real. Not least because last season’s cult hero loanee forward Joe Gelhardt has signed permanently from Leeds. Louise Taylor

Key ins: Nobel Mendy (Rayo Vallecano, £20m), Konstantinos Tzolakis (Olympiakos, £20m), Lucas Herrington (Colorado Rapids, £17.1m), Ilyas Ansah (Union Berlin, £14.5m), Mohamed-Ali Cho (Nice, £13m), Brooke Norton-Cuffy (Genoa, £12m), Jens Hjerto-Dahl (Tromsø, £10m), Tim Iroegbunam (Everton, £13m), Christos Mouzakitis (Olympiakos, £12.9m), Sorba Thomas (Stoke, £7.5m), Joe Gelhardt (Leeds, £6.5m), Jack Butland (Rangers, £3.5m), Lucas Gourna-Douath (Red Bull Salzburg, £3.4m), Elliot Stroud (Mjällby, £3m), Robinio Vaz (Roma, loan), Hidemasa Morita (Sporting, free), Matt Targett (Newcastle, free), Óscar Zambrano (Maribor, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Ivor Pandur (Rangers, £6m), Cody Drameh (Genoa, £3.9m), Abu Kamara (Portsmouth, £2.5m), Kyle Joseph (Middlesbrough, undisclosed fee)

The late addition of Burnley’s striker Zian Flemming brought Ipswich’s summer spend close to £200m. That appears to be the cost of giving yourselves a genuine shot at survival. Arrivals such as Exequiel Palacios and Julio Enciso should have no business in the lower reaches, and the former Fulham pair Sasa Lukic and Issa Diop add crucial experience. Gary O’Neil can call upon enviable depth in midfield and speed on the flanks, where Abdul Fatawu and Daizen Maeda look sharp. But time will tell whether Ipswich strengthened their defence sufficiently for regular tests of the kind they failed at Old Trafford on Sunday. Nick Ames

Key ins: Julio Enciso (Strasbourg, £26m), Emersonn (Toulouse, £24m), Exequiel Palacios (Bayer Leverkusen, £23.5m), Zian Flemming (Burnley, £20m), Abdul Fatawu (Leicester, £20m), Abdoul Ouattara (Strasbourg, £17m), Florentino Luís (Burnley, £16m), Daizen Maeda (Celtic, £10m), Sasa Lukic (Fulham, £9m), Kjell Scherpen (Union St-Gilloise, £8.6m), Issa Diop (Fulham, £8.5m), Chuba Akpom (Ajax, £7m), Kayne van Oevelen (Volendam, £3.4m), Cédric Kipré (Reims, £1.7m)

Key outs: George Hirst (Stoke, £6m), Arijanet Muric (Sassuolo, £6m), Harry Clarke (Preston, £3.5m)

In an ideal world Daniel Farke might have wished for one more high-calibre attacking recruit but that should not detract from a very decent window, featuring seven extremely sensible signings. The importance of the acquisition of the England goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City should not be underestimated. Trafford will almost certainly provide Leeds with a few more extra points – not to mention enhance their play courtesy of his stellar footwork. Just in front of him Tarik Muharemovic looks an outstanding defensive buy. Harry Wilson raises creativity levels and the attacking tone. LT

Key ins: James Trafford (Manchester City, £40.5m), Tarik Muharemovic (Sassuolo, £34.1m), Nico Elvedi (Borussia Mönchengladbach, £6.8m), Michael Zetterer (Eintracht Frankfurt, £4.3m), Jean-Mattéo Bahoya (Eintracht Frankfurt, loan), Melvin Bard (Nice, loan), Harry Wilson (Fulham, free)

Key outs: Pascal Struijk (Brighton, £18m), Joe Gelhardt (Hull, £6.5m), Lucas Perri (Torino, loan), Sebastiaan Bornauw (Hamburg, loan), Joël Piroe (West Ham, loan), Illan Meslier (Arsenal, free)

The final window of Richard Hughes’s spell as sporting director raised more questions over Liverpool’s direction under Fenway Sports Group, owners soon to be enriched by a £2bn investment from 1892 Holdings. The shift towards paying big money for big names continued with Bradley Barcola’s arrival from Paris Saint-Germain while Jérémy Jacquet and Victor Muñoz followed the older policy of developing young potential. Yet weaknesses remain at right back, defensive midfield and on the right wing, where Mohamed Salah’s exit was foreseen from December. Squad depth is lacking and a lot rests on the return to full fitness of Hugo Ekitiké, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni. AH

Key ins: Bradley Barcola (PSG, £123m), Jérémy Jacquet (Rennes, £55m), Víctor Muñoz (Osasuna, £34.5m), Ronald Araújo (Barcelona, loan)

Key outs: Curtis Jones (Inter, £25.7m), Harvey Elliott (Valencia, loan), Mohamed Salah (Trabzonspor, free), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid, free), Andy Robertson (Tottenham, free)

With Enzo Fernández’s deadline day signing for a British record-equalling £125m, Enzo Maresca can have zero complaints about a first window as Manchester City’s head coach. The No 8 follows two No 6s, in Elliot Anderson (£116m) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (£85m), and the wide players Allan Elias (£34m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£60m plus £5m) as major signings, the total spend on incomings about £457.5m. Factor in how City have generated about £281.8m in outgoings for a net spend of £175.7m, the divisions third-biggest of the window, and this sizable investment has to work - particularly the acquisition of Fernández. Jamie Jackson

Key ins: Enzo Fernández (Chelsea, £125m), Elliot Anderson (Nottingham Forest, £116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (Lille, £85.7m), Iliman Ndiaye (Everton, £60m), Allan (Palmeiras, £32m), Mathys Detourbet (Troyes, £21.6m), Gerónimo Rulli (Marseille, £1.7m)

Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free)

This was the window of the midfielder for Manchester United, with three recruited: Youri Tielemans (a No 8), Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba (No 6s). Yet missing was a left-back despite the targeting of Lewis Hall, and others, plus reinforcements for the rest of a creaking rearguard. The reason? A lack of money or, maybe, a reluctance to spend unless the finance was generated by transfers. Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury (preventing his sale) and Joshua Zirkzee’s reluctance to move were factors. Will the specialist Luke Shaw, plus the stand-in options of Parick Dorgu (a wing-back/left forward), Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui (right-backs), Lizandro Martínez (centre-back) and Baleba prove adequate? JJ

Key ins: Carlos Baleba (Brighton, £70m), Andrey Santos (Chelsea, £50m), Youri Tielemans (Aston Villa, £35m)

Key outs: Rasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m), Casemiro (Inter Miami, free)

Newcastle describe their transfer window as “transformative” and, with reinvention the name of the game on Tyneside, it is easy to see why. After selling Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães for a grand total not too far off £250m, they have signed eight – mainly young – players. Along the way the spine of a team now managed by Matthias Jaissle rather than Eddie Howe has been renewed and new cult heroes including the former Benfica right-back Amar Dedic and the former Manchester City midfielder Nico González are emerging. The deadline day arrival of the exciting 21-year-old Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille is regarded as quite a coup. Have Newcastle choreographed a triumph from a window that, at one point, looked potentially disastrous? LT

Key ins: Nico González (Manchester City, £52m), Matias Fernandez-Pardo (Lille, £51m), Bazoumana Touré (Hoffenheim, £43m), Aladji Bamba (Monaco, £30m), Amar Dedic (Benfica, £29.5m), Lukas Hornicek (Braga, £25.7m), Ewen Jaouen (Reims, £21.6m), Sean Steur (Ajax, £20m)

Receiving £116m for Elliot Anderson was proof that among the chaos in recent years, Forest have carried out some smart recruitment. After appointing Oliver Glasner, the club worked to provide for his needs, splashing out on Ousmane Diomande, while Xaver Schalger was a sensible acquisition for free, as was Daniel Muñoz at £22m. A No 9 was the priority and it required a club record £45m to acquire the long-term target Liam Delap, who fits the bill perfectly. Whether not sourcing a direct replacement for Anderson will hurt them remains to be seen but at least they did not panic, making it a measured window where they were able to trim the squad. Will Unwin

After last summer’s 14 new faces this had been a bit of a conservative, almost slightly underwhelming, window. Or at least it was until Crystal Palace tried to hijack Sunderland’s agreement to sign the Lyon winger Malick Fofana and the two Premier League clubs engaged in an astonishing deadline day tug of war involving private jets from both sitting on the tarmac at Lyon airport and Fofana undergoing a medical in France unsure as to his destination until finally choosing Wearside. Arguably Sunderland’s biggest achievement was keeping last season’s star players. If persuading Granit Xhaka to stay rather than defect to Chelsea was vital, Régis Le Bris will be similarly delighted to have retained widely admired individuals of the calibre of Enzo Le Fée, Robin Roefs and Noah Sadiki. LT

A comprehensive reboot, from back to front, featuring a club record outlay for a window and one of the most lavish by any club ever. In the first summer window since the departure of the longstanding chair Daniel Levy, the hierarchy have backed Roberto De Zerbi in an attempt to put the trauma of last season behind them. All the new signings have Premier League experience and – apart from Mateus Fernandes and Sávio – are aged 25 or over. In other words, they ought to be ready to hit the ground running. The opening two matches did not go to plan. It will get better. Won’t it? David Hytner

#934. Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Some of Brazil’s wildlife have traces of plastic circulating in their blood — even if they live far from land used by humans, according to an analysis published on 11 November in Nature1.

Researchers measured the concentration of microplastics in the blood of 47 animals: 26 lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) and 21 giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla). The scientists found that, on average, the creatures carry similar levels of plastic as many humans — roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood. The animals that lived closest to human infrastructure and waste-management facilities had the highest levels of microplastics in their blood.

But even those living more than 100 kilometres from a waste sites and 65 kilometres from human infrastructure showed traces of the pollutants. This indicates that plastics can reach wildlife living far from where the pollution originates, says study co-author Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz, a conservation scientist at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus in Kelowna, Canada.

The findings are an important step to better understand how the particles impact wildlife, says Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou, a geochemist at the National Taiwan University in Taipei.

Microplastics are tiny particles (smaller than five millimetres across) with many different chemical compositions. They can travel through the environment in rainwater, rivers and the atmosphere. Although several studies have measured microplastics levels in wildlife, few have explored how the surrounding environment influences what animals ingest, says study co-author Michael Noonan, a quantitative ecologist at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus.

To find out, Noonan, Ferraz and their colleagues collected and analysed blood samples from animals living across the Amazon rainforest, the Cerrado savannah and the huge and pristine Pantanal wetland between February 2021 and November 2022. The researchers also used GPS data to track the animals’ movements and their exposure to a human footprint.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03660-5

Ferraz, M. A. M. M. et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x (2026).

#933. What can you read into Premier League table after 10 games?

Only four teams have taken more points than Arsenal's 27 after 10 games

We are now more than a quarter of the way through the Premier League season, with each team having played 10 games.

History suggests the answer is quite a lot.

Last season, for instance, the top two - and two of the eventual bottom three - were in the exact spots at this stage that they in finished six months later.

How the Premier League table looks after 10 games

Arsenal are top of the table on 27 points - which is higher than the average number of points (23) champions have after 10 games.

In fact, only four teams have taken more points from their first 10 fixtures than the Gunners, and all four have gone on to win the league.

One small quirk that means Arenal fans should not start making plans for a parade just yet is that the only two previous sides to post exactly 27 points at this point of the campaign both failed to win the title - including the Gunners in 2022-23.

In 15 of the 34 Premier League seasons to date, the team top at this stage have gone on to win the title, so less than half the time.

While on 16 previous occasions, teams on 22 points, the tally of second-placed Brighton, or fewer after 10 games won the title, so there is still hope for the Seagulls.

However, the less good news for Fabian Hurzeler's side is that, bizarrely, the team in second after 10 games have won the title in just one of the past 18 seasons - that was Manchester City in 2022-23.

The fewest points any side has had at this stage and gone on to win the league is 18 - so City, on 21, and Liverpool, on 18, could still have a say.

Arsenal lead Brighton by five points, one fewer than the most points a team have ever come from behind at this stage to win a title.

Manchester United in 2002-03 and Manchester City in 2013-14 are the two to do that.

But Mikel Arteta and co can take comfort knowing the leaders at this stage have gone on to win the title in the past two seasons - after failing to do so in the previous four years.

Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Odegaard spare VAR blushes?

Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top

Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit

Crystal Palace are propping up the table having lost their past four league matches, but the stats suggest their position is far from terminal.

In total, 14 teams have stayed up having been bottom of the table at this point in the season - most recently Wolves in 2024-25.

Moreover, the fewest points a team has had after 10 games and stayed up at the end of the season is three.

That same Wolves team are the most recent of the four teams to have achieved that feat.

Sunderland, who climbed off the foot of the table with victory over Chelsea, had just four points at this stage in 2013-14 but still ended up finishing 14th.

Palace can also count themselves a little unfortunate to have amassed seven points and find themselves in 20th.

Only Bolton in 2002-03 have had more points (eight) after 10 games and been bottom - and that was in a situation when a number of other sides had played 11 matches.

Overall, 88 teams have previously had seven or fewer points after 10 Premier League games and 37 managed to stay up.

There is good news for Ipswich and Hull in that every promoted side since 2015-16 to take 11 points or more from their first 10 games - and there have been 14 of them - has survived.

The most recent promoted side to make as bright a start and go down were Cardiff in 2013-14, who were 12th with 12 points but finished bottom on 30 points.

The outlook is a little bleaker for Coventry.

Only two promoted sides in the past 11 seasons have taken fewer than 11 points and survived - Bournemouth in 2015-16 (eight) and Nottingham Forest in 2022-23 (five).

Frank Lampard's men are also the seventh promoted side to take exactly nine points from their first 10 games - two of the previous six survived (Wolves in 2009-10 and Leicester in 2014-15).

Lampard feels hair pull should have led to Coventry penalty

A long way to go then, still plenty of time for things to change. But how much do things really change from this point?

Well, not a great deal if we look at last season, when 15 of the 20 teams finished within three places of where they were after 10 games.

Aston Villa made the biggest jump, going from 11th at this stage to secure a top-four finish with time to spare.

So Champions League qualification remains well within grasp for Unai Emery's side, who are currently in 10th.

On the other extreme were Tottenham, riding high in sixth after 10 games before plummeting 11 places down the standings to finishing 17th, only securing survival on the final day.

As mentioned earlier, the top two and two of the eventual bottom three were already in their final positions by this point, while Burnley - the third relegated side - were only a place above the drop zone in 17th.

Perhaps Manchester United are in a relegation battle after all...?

#931. How Germany's greatest goalscorer is guiding the next generation

Miroslav Klose's FC Nuremberg side sit second in the 2. Bundesliga

It is no surprise Miroslav Klose recognises the value of a true goalscorer.

He is, after all, Germany's all-time leading marksman and until this summer had netted more than any other player in men's World Cup history. Even now, only Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi can top his 16 across four tournaments.

But of the more than 300 goals Klose scored in a career that began in Germany's amateur leagues and spanned Kaiserslautern, Werder Bremen, Bayern Munich and Lazio, he reckons all but two came inside the penalty area.

"Thankfully, we've moved away a little from the idea of the false nine or having a second striker playing around the main striker, with everyone coming towards the ball," explains the FC Nuremberg boss.

"For me, the most important thing is that you need someone who is there to score goals. You need someone in the box because that's where you're closest to the goal. That's why I'm a big believer in practising the final ball, whether it's a cross, a shot or something else.

"That's crucial. How do you create that final ball? When you develop automatisms and players get to know each other better, that's when you see harmony on the pitch.

"It can make things look effortless, but it involves a huge amount of work. A lot of work in training and attention to detail, making sure the players communicate with each other and understand their team-mates' strengths and weaknesses."

That focus on detail stems from Klose's diligence during his playing days. He would study opponents' movement, analyse a goalkeeper's position and shape when facing certain shots - do they make themselves big? Are their hands high or low?

"When goals are scored, the whole team deserves credit," adds the 48-year-old, who was as selfless as he was ruthless. "But you still need someone who has that ability in their feet or in their head to put the ball in the net."

"He's a great role model for me" - Former German forward on Harry Kane

Klose was 36 when he won the World Cup with Germany in 2014 - surpassing Ronaldo's goal record in a 7-1 semi-final thrashing of hosts Brazil.

It was the culmination of a career built on hard work after a series of near-misses - something that may offer solace to Harry Kane and England that a major tournament triumph remains possible.

Born in communist Poland, Klose's father Josef - also a footballer, most notably for Auxerre - moved the family to West Germany when his son was eight.

He was never in a big academy, playing in the lower leagues while training as a carpenter before eventually joining Kaiserslautern.

Klose, like Kane, was in his early 20s by the time he established himself in top-flight football, but just two years after his Bundesliga debut was starting a World Cup final defeat by Brazil.

The striker, 38 when he hung up his goalscoring boots, admires the way Kane has evolved as he has matured, using him as an example to his own young prospects.

"You could always see his quality, and he's worked incredibly hard to get where he is," says Klose of the Ballon d'Or winner.

"He's also a great role model for me, particularly because he has stayed in Germany. I often tell my players that they should look at someone like him as an example.

"Young players can't yet have the instinct and experience he has developed, but that's where it starts - thinking about what you can and can't do as a footballer. You have to keep learning. That's the crucial thing for me.

"If you understand that you train to become better, then in five years' time you'll naturally be a different player. But if you think everything will happen automatically just because 10 people around you tell you that you're a fantastic player, I don't think you'll continue to develop."

Klose's Nuremberg have the youngest average age in the 2. Bundesliga

Klose has a knack for working with young talent, previously coaching Bayern Munich's under-17s. His Nuremberg side are the youngest in the German second tier with an average age of 23.3 years, according to Transfermarkt.

"You need that balance and a certain core of experienced players," he explains. "But we're very brave in that respect. Over the three years I've been here, we've made progress in how we assess young players and in the conversations we have about them.

"How do we rate them? How far along are they? What do they need to work on to take the next step? Is it perhaps more about their physical development? Because from a footballing perspective, we're already producing some really good players."

Klose's coaching journey began with the national team before he joined Bayern, briefly becoming Hansi Flick's assistant, and then took his first managerial role at Rheindorf Altach in Austria.

He joined Nuremberg, historically one of Germany's most successful clubs, in 2024 and steered them to 10th and eighth-placed finishes.

This season they sit second, behind Hertha BSC, and are the league's joint-top scorers, with eyes on a return to the Bundesliga for the first time since 2019.

"When I first arrived, I spoke to the youth coaches about the club's DNA and its coaching philosophy, and what they focus on," adds Klose.

"There was already a lot of common ground. We suggested trying certain things because we wanted to do a little more in particular areas, and they were open to that.

"That's important. We benefit from this because our young players are getting opportunities in the first team, and everyone is paying attention to their development.

"But that journey starts with the youth coaches. I know how important it is to take those steps. We're benefiting from that now because we have access to so many young talents.

"As a coaching team, we're brave enough to give them opportunities when we see that they can compete at this level. That's the first step."

Among the 11 to play the most minutes for Klose's side this season, seven are 22 years old or under, including top scorer Mohamed Ali Zoma, already capped by Italy.

"Of course, everyone gets a lot of praise, as is currently the case with Marc Kornwachs," says Klose of a 17-year-old midfielder also catching the eye.

"But his journey isn't over yet. Now it's about helping him become more consistent and establishing himself, while continuing to develop his game and take further steps forward.

"These players are so talented that we have absolutely no hesitation in giving them opportunities, regardless of the scoreline."

Klose was still playing fifth-tier amateur football aged 20 before becoming the World Cup's all-time top goalscorer in 2014

Klose also understands his managerial career is still young - mirroring the humble nature that earned him fair play awards in Germany and Italy.

"I'm very comfortable with the steps I've taken, even though it involves a huge amount of work," he says about his progress. "You learn something every day.

"I've said that I'm already a much better manager than I was three years ago. That's perfectly normal, and you have to embrace it. I've always been willing and eager to learn, and I've always been a hard worker. That isn't going to change."

So what does a Miroslav Klose team look like?

"Personally, as a player, I always liked having the ball for long periods, and that hasn't changed," he explains.

"When you have the ball, you have a certain level of dominance. I know you also have to be very adaptable in terms of possession, and that's something we are. We constantly show the players different ways of playing out of situations.

"It's great to see how they develop and to be able to support individual players along the way. That's exactly the approach I like to take as a manager."

#926. Referee observer banned for discriminatory comments

Brian Curson has been involved in football for more than 40 years

A Pro Ref referee observer has been suspended for nine weeks and fined Â£200 for making discriminatory remarks after a match he was working at.

Brian Curson had visited Kenilworth Road to assess the officials at the League One fixture between Luton Town and Rotherham United on 15 November 2025.

An allegation was made that Curson made two discriminatory comments in the lounge at Luton's stadium after the game, which led to the Football Association investigation.

Curson was charged with acting in an improper manner and/or using abusive and/or insulting words.

It was considered an 'aggravated breach', using words which included a reference - whether express or implied - to ethnic origin, race or nationality.

Curson, who no longer works for Pro Ref, said that he did not recall making the comments but the FA commission "was satisfied on the balance of probabilities" that they had been made.

The FA requested a time-based sanction because of Curson's role in the sport, as a player would serve a suspension of between nine and 12 matches.

It was determined that, taking into account Curson's experience and role on the day of the match, he should be suspended for nine weeks.

Curson was also told he must attend a mandatory education programme, and received a warning as to future conduct.

#924. From Jersey to Somalia... via Liverpool & Man City

Somalia midfielder Jarma Mohamed moved to eighth-tier Jersey Bulls in the summer

Not many 21-year-olds can say they have played international football, had spells at Liverpool and Manchester City and are now playing in non-league after being spotted on a mobile app.

But Jarma Mohamed's footballing journey is not that of your typical midfielder.

The combative playmaker has been recalled to Somalia's side for their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with Ghana this month, capping a rollercoaster year for the Liverpudlian.

"My mum was probably fed up with me just booting stuff in the house, so she got me involved as early as I could," Mohamed jokes with BBC Sport as he talks about the start of his footballing journey.

"When I was three she was begging teams to take me because the age that you're allowed is four.

"Eventually someone saw me playing and it turned out to be an Everton scout, so I ended up playing for Everton from four and then at that age between four to nine you can play for a few teams.

"It was at Liverpool and Everton, eventually chose Liverpool at nine, then signed for Man City at 11.

"I came out of Man City and got a scholarship at Wigan, which is one of the best memories of playing football, having a two-year deal, playing day-in, day-out, full-time schedule, staying in digs up in Wigan, travelling up and down the country for away games, performing, picking up the armband a few times, FA Youth Cup, things like that."

Jersey Bulls' midfielder Mohamed wins historic call-up

Jersey Bulls sign Somalia midfielder Mohamed

Mohamed featured alongside players including Jayden Danns at Liverpool and England stars Rico Lewis and Nico O'Reilly at Manchester City.

He was released by Wigan in 2024 and spent time in non-league football with Bamber Bridge and Newcastle Town.

His career came to a crossroads in the summer, when Isthmian League South Central side Jersey Bulls spotted him on an app for footballers.

"I was thinking what do I want to do?," he said.

"I could go abroad and do something, but I wasn't really too sure and I'd been playing showcase games with a company called Player, who basically put players in front of teams, they have an app, which is like a LinkedIn for footballers.

"Jersey Bulls were on the app looking for players and, long story short, the owner of Player put me in contact with Jersey Bulls.

"I know the club's amateur and no-one gets paid, but we worked out a job that aligns with the things that I do, obviously me having Uefa C licence coaching is something that I'd easily do and I've come over and done it."

Jarma Mohamed and his Jersey Bulls team-mates have yet to lose a league game this season

Mohamed now works as a youth coach in the island, while also anchoring the midfield of a Jersey Bulls side riding high in the eighth tier of English football.

Born in Toxteth, Mohamed's Somalian grandfather moved to Liverpool, part of a large Somali community in the city.

It is that heritage that has allowed him to play for a side ranked 200th in the world - the lowest of any team to progress to Afcon 2027's final round of qualifiers.

He made his Somalia debut against Mauritius in March as the Ocean Stars reached the final qualifying stages for Afcon for the first time in their history - they beat the island nation on penalties after two goalless draws.

"It was a random Wednesday afternoon in my kitchen and I was made up," Mohamed says of the moment he was asked to first join the Somalia squad earlier this year.

"I could physically see the community close to home, and going out to the camp and experiencing what that's like, it really lit a fire that I didn't even know I could get as far as trying to push my football career."

He is part of a Somali squad made up of more players from the global diaspora than those born in the country itself.

Having reached the qualifying stage for next year's tournament, the lowest ranked side left face a tough group against three-time champions Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Ghana - who have won the tournament four times and drew 0-0 with England in the group stage of this summer's World Cup.

"Everyone's from different parts of the world, you have lads who are Dutch, from Finland, Italy, there's another scouse with me in the team," Mohamed said.

"When we're all there, and even lads who are local and playing in the Somali league, everyone's just one family.

"That's one thing which we're really good at, we're together as a team, there's no egos.

"Everyone's just really together and wanting to get results for the country, which I feel is very important."

Somalia were narrowly beaten by the Ivory Coast in September

In their first two qualifying matches Somalia have not let themselves down.

The Gambia scored an 83rd-minute winner to overcome them in their opening game, while an Ivory Coast side boasting Real Madrid's summer signing Yan Diomande, Atalanta's Franck Kessie and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pepe scored in the 89th minute and the fifth minute of added time to earn a 2-0 win.

It means the Somalis are second from bottom in Group C on goal difference, above a Ghana side who have Kim Bjorkegren in interim charge after the Black Stars lost their opening two matches under Carlos Queiroz.

With the tense security situation in Somalia, the Ocean Stars have played all their qualifiers away from home and will face Ghana in back-to-back matches in Takoradi.

So how will Mohamed, who plays in front of sparse crowds in small grounds in the area south of London, approach facing opponents who ply their trade in the biggest leagues in the world?

"The same way I treat every game, you can only play what's in front of you," he added.

"If you play the name or an occasion you're losing before you've even kicked a ball.

"I just play who's in front of me and keep it at that.

"You know the players' levels, the qualities that they have that you have to respect, but you also have to back yourself.

"You're sharing the same pitch for a reason, it's not by accident."

And can the Ocean Stars make next year's tournament in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania?

"If you come to do nothing less than that you may as well stay home.

"In the two games we've had previously against Ivory Coast and Gambia we've shown that we can compete.

"If you come to play for the experience or 'we're just happy to be there', then there's no point in coming.

#921. From W-M to the No 10, shirt numbers tell a story of football’s tactical evolution

In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, as well as the attributes a player was supposed to demonstrate

Ultimate 1-50: check out our complete list of players

Numbers have a fascination. The No 10 is revered almost everywhere, but perhaps most especially in Argentina, where it denotes the playmaker, the enganche, the quasi-mythical figure who links the front and back of the team. Liverpool and Manchester United have reasons to celebrate their No 7. Ajax retired No 14 for Johan Cruyff, Milan their No 3 and No 6 for Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi respectively and Birmingham their 22 for Jude Bellingham as gestures of respect for their abilities. Other numbers have been retired to mark premature deaths: the No 20 at Liverpool for Diogo Jota, the No 23 at Manchester City for Marc-Vivian Foé, the 21 at Espanyol for Daniel Jarque.

But numbers are not just about individuals. In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, and the expectations of particular numbers in particular cultures, as well as the attributes a player in that shirt was supposed to demonstrate, themselves tell a story of tactical evolution.

The earliest evidence of teams wearing numbered shirts seems to be in a game between the Australian sides Sydney Leichhardt and HSM Powerful in 1911. The University of Chicago’s American football team wore squad numbers in 1913. There were experiments with numbers on sleeves in baseball from 1916. There were isolated efforts with numbered shirts in the American Soccer League, which began in 1923, and, especially, in the USA’s Challenge Cup. Various touring sides began to experiment with numbered shirts through the 1920s and, in August 1928, on the opening day of the English league season, two games featured numbers. Chelsea’s outfielders wore 2-11 in their Second Division game against Swansea, while Sheffield Wednesday wore 1-11 and Arsenal 12-22 in a First Division clash at Hillsborough.

Similarly, 1-22 numbering was used in the 1933 FA Cup final, in part because Everton and Manchester City were forced to wear change kits due to a colour clash, although the presence of the touring West Indies cricket side, who were not expected to be familiar with the individual players, was also cited. It wasn’t until June 1939, though, that the Football League took a vote to introduce squad numbers. It passed 24-20, and it was decided both teams should wear 1-11, but in strict order, as though the formation had been laid out on a page with the goalkeeper at the top.

This was complicated by the fact that, although almost every team by that stage had responded to the 1925 change in the offside law by adopting the W-M formation (a 3-2-2-3), there was still a belief that the “right” way to play was a 2-3-5. Thus the goalkeeper wore No 1, the right-back No 2, the left-back No 3, the right-half No 4, the centre-half No 5 and so on up to the centre-forward in No 9, the inside-left in No 10 and the left-winger in No 11. In practice, though, the centre-half (5), played between the full-backs (2 and 3) while the inside-forwards (8 and 10) played deeper than the wingers and centre-forward (7, 9 and 11).

Numbers rapidly became sacrosanct. When Hungary came to Wembley in 1953 and became the first foreign side to beat England at the national stadium, they provoked consternation because they were “incorrectly” numbered. The centre-back Mihaly Lantos wore No 4. The midfield creator Jozsef Bozsik wore No 5. Most bafflingly of all, Nandor Hidegkuti, the No 9, didn’t play as a centre-forward but created from midfield. What was Harry Johnston, England’s hapless centre-half, to do? Convention said he, the No 5, should pick up the No 9, but if he did that he left a huge hole in the back line. And if he did not, Hidegkuti was free to pick England apart.

The introspection provoked by that defeat led within a decade or so to a number of leading English teams adopting a back four, usually by withdrawing the left-half (the No 6) into the defensive line. As Alf Ramsey’s 1966 World Cup winners showed the value of packing midfield, so the wingers dropped back, leaving a 4-4-2 that lined up: 1; 2, 5, 6, 3; 7, 4, 8, 11; 9, 10. Within that, the No 4 would usually be the more defensive of the two central midfielders, while the No 10 retained some of the qualities of the inside-left, which is to say he tended to be the smaller, more creative forward alongside a big, physical number No 9.

Other countries, though, followed a different path. In Argentina, for instance, there had been no sudden shift to W-M in the late 1920s but, at River Plate in the late 1930s, the right-half Norberto Yácono, nicknamed “the Stamp” for his tight marking, would pick up the opposing creator. As other teams followed the principle, the number No 4 became a de facto third back, but operating on the right. No 4 remains the standard number for an Argentinian right-back, as exemplified by Javier Zanetti, for whom Inter retired the shirt. When Argentina switched to a back four after the humiliation of the 6-1 defeat to Czechoslovakia at the 1958 World Cup, the left-half fell into the back line, so a standard Argentinian back four would read: 4, 2, 6, 3. The No 5 remained as the caudillo in midfield, almost as venerated as the No 10 in the form of Antonio Rattín, Américo Gallego and Javier Mascherano.

In Brazil, though, there had been no widespread conversion of the right-half into a right-back, and so when the back four was adopted, the wing-halves simply dropped either side of the full-backs, leaving a standard back four as: 4, 2, 3, 6. The great right-back Carlos Alberto, for instance, wore No 4 at the 1970 World Cup, while the left-back Roberto Carlos tended to wear No 6. When, at Flamengo in the 1940s, Flávio Costa tipped the midfield square of Dori Kürschner’s W-M to create his diagonal, a major step towards 4-2-4, the No 5 became the more defensive central midfielder – leading to players such as Clodoaldo, Mauro Silva and Casemiro wearing the shirt for the national team – while the inside-left, the No 10, became the most creative midfielder.

In other countries, other conventions emerged. It was in the Netherlands and West Germany that the standard delineations of the expectations on midfielders in a 4-3-3 emerged. The No 6 would be the deep-lying player, the No 10 would be the creator, and the No 8 would be a box-to-box player shuttling between them. Or in France, where a five-man bench from which a manger could use two substitutes was adopted in 1976, it became standard for the reserve goalkeeper to wear No 16. Many goalkeepers in the Francophone world gained their first experience wearing No 16 and so favoured it when squad numbers were introduced: that’s why Fabian Barthez wore No 16 at the 1998 World Cup and Cameroon’s Thomas N’Kono wore it in 1990.

Numbers now are often a matter of personal choice and of brand-building. In a squad system, players can take on a familiar number and hope to embody its spirit, or try to make a more obscure number their own, as Johan Cruyff did with the No 14 more than half a century ago.

Numbers have a past, and they tell a story. Nobody on the Football League committee that narrowly voted to mandate squad numbers in 1939 would have considered the possibility, but in numbers are written the deep history of a country’s tactical development.

#919. Vinicius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs

Watch: VinÃ­cius Jr's surprise message to boy who received prosthetic legs after Sudan drone strike

In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.

The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger VinÃ­cius JÃºnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.

Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.

We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.

More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.

Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.

More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.

In his video message, Real Madrid star VinÃ­cius Jr invited Zaher to watch a Real Madrid match together

The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was VinÃ­cius JÃºnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

VinÃ­cius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new VinÃ­cius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell VinÃ­cius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

Zaher is one of millions of children whose lives have been devastated by Sudan's civil war

Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.

Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.

Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.

"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.

She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."

Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.

Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.

"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.

There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.

Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising Â£45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.

Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.

Zaher has learned to use his new legs with months of support from doctors and physiotherapists in Cairo

After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.

For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.

"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."

His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.

As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.

He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.

For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.

Khartoum has suffered extensive damage, with many buildings damaged and their contents stolen

The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.

Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".

"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.

Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.

Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb

#918. Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap

Obsessive attention to detail is helping striker to reach new heights – and a 126th international appearance on Thursday

It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September.

No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-blowing?

The bottom line was that there was a gain. So Kane did what he has always done – he leaned into it. Strongly. As the goals flowed as never before, he said it became “addictive”. The 33-year-old striker finished the season with 61 goals for Bayern Munich and 12 for England. According to data from Gradient Sports, his sprints and accelerations per 90 minutes for Bayern were up significantly on 2024-25. This season, he has 10 goals for Bayern and six for England. Again, his sprint and acceleration statistics have improved.

It is a window into Kane’s mentality, the insatiable quest for self‑improvement, the fixation with details large and small, which was the basis for his Ballon d’Or coronation two weeks ago. It is why, as he prepares to make his 126th England appearance against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night and overtake Peter Shilton as the nation’s most capped men’s player, it is hard to argue that he is not getting better with age.

Kane is the ultimate modern‑day professional, who controls everything he can control. The no‑sweets choice is the most recent on a dietary journey that started more than 10 years ago when he began to work with the nutritional specialist Dan Sargeant.

Kane had his meals prepared by Sargeant, who believes that everyone has a different reaction to food and analyses everything from bone broths to the white bits on oranges to tailor individual plans. Kane has not worked directly with Sargeant since his transfer from Tottenham to Bayern in 2023 – he has a different chef in Munich – but he continues to follow his advice.

It is common knowledge that Kane is teetotal during the season, albeit he had a few drinks as he celebrated his Ballon d’Or triumph. It was the first and almost certainly the last time he broke his rule. Similarly, everyone is aware of Kane’s obsession with recovery after games; his use of ice baths and infrared saunas. He also places great store in the quality of his sleep.

Less well-known is the depth of his relationship with his private doctor, Alejandro Elorriaga Claraco, who specialises in electrical neurofunctional acupuncture. Kane started seeing the Spaniard on a recommendation from the golfer Justin Rose after sustaining a severe hamstring tear playing for Spurs in 2020.

Claraco is based in Canada but travels to see Kane and spends at least a week every month with him. During that time, he will treat Kane on a table for four to five hours each day, getting his muscles pumping with acupuncture needles hooked up to a small battery. Claraco has been fundamental in helping Kane to understand his body; what he can and cannot do, plus how he gets over injuries.

Kane is hurtling towards his record-breaking England cap. He is in better shape than ever; mentally, as well, because he has grown so much as a leader and public speaker, particularly over the past few years of his England captaincy. He was given the armband on a full-time basis by Gareth Southgate in 2018, the fulfilment of a boyhood dream.

Kane has never hidden the fact that England is his priority, mainly because he was such a fan of the national team as a boy. It will be an emotional occasion for him against Croatia and his journey will flash before him. It began with the goal on his debut against Lithuania in 2015, 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for Wayne Rooney, and it is worth dwelling on the numbers.

Of Kane’s 91 goals – an England record – 21 have come at major tournaments: 14 at World Cups, seven at European Championships. Only two European players have more combined goals at World Cup tournaments and European Championships: Cristiano Ronaldo (25) and Kylian Mbappé (23). Kane has scored 12 times in the knockout rounds. As an aside, he has 21 assists for England, which puts him joint‑second on the all-time men’s list with Steven Gerrard, behind David Beckham (39).

The best moments? Kane is very fond of the Lithuania goal, not to mention the last-gasp winner against Tunisia in the 2018 World Cup group stage and the clincher against Germany in the last 16 at Euro 2020. He always says that one of his best England performances was against Ukraine in the quarter-final of that tournament, when he scored twice. More recently, there were the two goals that saved the day against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup last summer.

Kane’s penalties are a major part of his England story. His record shows 26 successes and five misses, although he scored on the rebound against Denmark in the Euro 2020 semi-final. His conversion against the Netherlands in the Euro 2024 semi-final involved withstanding incredible pressure. Ditto the one against Mexico in the last 16 of this past World Cup. The scar that will never heal was the miss in the 2-1 World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in Qatar in 2022. Was it the low point of his career? Kane is on record as saying the World Cup semi-final exit against Argentina in the summer was worse.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

He was never supposed to make it this far; to reach the Hollywood moment of winning the Ballon d’Or, receiving the trophy from the Brazilian Ronaldo and giving an acceptance speech that tugged hard on the heartstrings. His voice wobbled as he paid tribute to his mother, Kim, who had tears in her eyes, and his father, Pat.

Kane was never a wonderkid at Spurs; he had difficult loans at Norwich and Leicester. He was doubted. It is true to say he has wrung every last drop from his talent; the dedication has underpinned everything. And yet the raw ability was always there, something often overlooked.

Harry Redknapp, the manager who gave Kane his Spurs debut in 2011, tells a story from the player’s formative days. It involved a behind-closed-doors game at the training ground against Birmingham, whose centre‑half Scott Dann was on the verge of a move to Arsenal. Birmingham included Dann in their team as he returned from a minor injury and Arsenal asked Redknapp whether they could come along to watch.

“I got a call from Pat Rice [the Arsenal assistant manager] and Steve Rowley [the chief scout] and I said: ‘Of course, no problem, come over,’” Redknapp said. “Arsenal were signing Scott Dann, they just wanted to check his fitness. So they came to watch and I think Harry scored four goals that day and Arsenal didn’t sign Scott Dann. Harry absolutely ran amok that day.

“We always felt Harry was going to be a player. No one could come here now and say we knew he was going to be England’s all-time record caps holder, record scorer and Ballon d’Or winner. Anyone who says that is talking rubbish. But we did think there was a player there. How good he would be, no one was ever sure.”

Kane was breathtaking when he broke through for Spurs and England in 2014-15 and there were people who thought that would be it; he was tagged as a one-season wonder. He has been a wonder in every season since, the dynamics finessed, perhaps, by the sense that nothing has been given to him; his humility, too.

There has never been the hint of scandal about Kane and it is perfectly possible that Haribos may be his biggest vice. The Ballon d’Or is the Boy Next d’Or and there was genuine happiness in all quarters when he won the award – not only among his friends in the game. That said, the reaction of his former Spurs teammate Son Heung‑min, who is at Los Angeles FC, was gold. He tore off on a goal celebration‑style run at his club’s training ground when he heard the news.

Where can Kane take this? When will it end? Nobody knows but two things are clear. He is equipped to keep pushing for a good number of years and it has long since passed the point where it is reasonable to doubt him.
