#853. Scott Disick Makes Rare Comments About Raising Mason Disick

Scott Disick shared rare insight into parenting his and ex Kourtney Kardashian's 16-year-old son, admitting that it's "scarier" than raising Penelope, 14, and Reign, 11.

Scott Disick is having a hard time keeping up with his teen.

The Kardashians star shared insight into how parenting his and ex Kourtney Kardashian's 16-year-old son Mason compares to raising his younger siblings Penelope, 14, and Reign, 11.

"I kind of consider Reign a little kid still 'cause I got Mace who's like an adult," Scott explained to Khloe Kardashian during the Nov. 12 Kardashians episode. "It's so much scarier."

"For instance, this past weekend, they were up all night out, went to some parties," he continued, "and I literally just sat on my phone and looked at Life360 and Find My app to see where Mace was until he got home—the whole night."

Meanwhile, Khloe—mom to kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Tristan Thompson—related to Scott's concerns about Mason, already worrying about her kids getting older.

"I will 100 percent track my kids," the Khloe in Wonder Land podcast host admitted during a confessional. "I would put a chip in my children to know where they are at all times."

"If it's safe, that's what I have to look into," she teased. "Why is this not suggested more? So, I'm a believer in things that maybe other people are not."

As for Scott, he and Kourtney—whom he dated on and off from 2006 to 2015—are partners in navigating their children through their teenage years. And even though the pair ultimately decided they were better suited to a platonic relationship, they still had to get their f--king asses up and work on their co-parenting.

As Kourtney previously admitted, "It's not easy," with the Poosh founder adding during her October 2025 confessional on The Kardashians, "I think, with co-parenting, it's always trying to be cordial, do our best to be on the same page."

Meanwhile, Scott has discussed how his bond with Kourtney—who also shares Rocky, 3, as well as stepchildren Atiana De La Hoya, 27, Landon Barker, 23, and Alabama Barker, 20, with husband Travis Barker—has been "one of the more difficult things" in his life.

"I always had her friends or our family in my ear kind of like, 'Don't worry, honey, eventually you guys will figure it out,'" he said during a 2022 episode of the reality show. "And, 'You'll get back together one day.' So my foot was always halfway in the door."

Though Scott is happy that Kourtney is doing amazing with her sweetie, whom she wed in 2022, he admitted that he was especially afraid of losing his relationship with the entire family.

"Feeling left out and not being told anything is super hurtful," he shared, noting, however, that when it came to seeing Travis and Kourtney together romantically, "I'd rather be around them and be around my family than not at all."

#852. How 'Barca way' continues despite big-name exits

Esmee Brugts has made more than 100 appearances for Barcelona after joining in 2023

Barcelona's team is markedly different to the one Arsenal faced in the 2025 Women's Champions League final - but the challenge is as difficult as ever.

Three-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas was among a number of high-profile summer departures, but Barca remain favourites to continue their European domination.

The reigning champions have won all three league-phase matches, scoring 19 goals, and welcome Arsenal to the Nou Camp on Thursday (17:45 GMT).

Two seasons ago, Arsenal stunned Barcelona in the Women's Champions League final, less than five months after Renee Slegers was named permanent manager.

That victory kick-started a new era for the Gunners under Slegers, but it has not gone to plan so far this season.

Disappointing results and a five-game winless run, which ended in October, have left Arsenal sixth in the Women's Super League.

However, the Gunners have started the European campaign well and are fifth in the table with seven points from their first three matches.

And given Barcelona's summer changes, Arsenal might have hoped to be facing a team in transition - but the Spanish giants look as strong as ever.

So how have Barca - who have won four of the past six Women's Champions League titles - hit the ground running this term despite losing some of their key players?

Nations League draw, BBC Womenâs Footballer of the Year & can Arsenal shock Barcelona again?

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

What is the Women's Champions League prize money?

When Spain great Putellas left Barcelona in the summer to join London City Lionesses, it felt like the end of an era.

She was followed to Bromley by defender Mapi Leon, while full-back Ona Batlle joined Arsenal and Salma Paralluelo swapped Barcelona for European rivals Lyon.

All four had played a key part in Barcelona's dominance and ended their time at the club with a historic quadruple, including a fourth Champions League last season.

So how have Barcelona coped with losing such big players?

"Every season is different. There are always changes but we know that's football," Barcelona's Esmee Brugts told BBC Sport.

"There's an opportunity to make a new story and that's up to us. So far, I've been quite happy with how it's going.

"I'm excited for the upcoming games to see how we do. It can be a bit different - but different in a good way also."

Barcelona's success is down to multiple factors, but it all centres around a distinctive playing identity that is ingrained in Spanish footballers from a young age.

Stars such as three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati were developed at the club's famous La Masia youth academy, situated next to the Estadi Johan Cruyff, which is named after one of Barca's greatest footballers.

They produce a conveyor belt of talent, all trained to play the same way, and having learned to swap in and out of positions seamlessly.

It is a way of playing that Netherlands international Brugts has picked up with ease since joining in 2023.

"It's difficult to explain because it's so many small things. It's doing the simple things good," said Brugts. "It's a team sport. If everybody does their own roles, you'll perform the best way.

"I watched a documentary about Johan Cruyff and it's exactly how he wanted to play. It's how we try to play every week. We try to be as perfect as possible.

"We try to win every trophy there is by playing really beautiful football, in my opinion. The 'tiki-taka' I enjoy so much."

Barcelona beat rivals Real Madrid 7-0 last month in Liga F

Arsenal boss Slegers said Barcelona have "a really strong identity" and she does not believe this changes when new players come into the side.

"They can play in different positions and also have a very strong and clear way of playing. It's very impressive with the way Barcelona plays," said Slegers.

"With new players coming in and then rotating, their style of play stands up. We think we have quite a clear idea of what that could look like."

While it is a new era for Barcelona, their ambitions remain the same - to defend their four titles this season.

Brugts said they are "really building" their identity with new players in the squad and believe there are "no limits" to what they can produce.

Talented youngsters such as midfielder Clara Serrajordi, 18, defender Renee van Asten, 20, and forward Vicky Lopez, 20, have added more depth to the squad.

"It took me some time to adjust, to learn and understand what it is to play the Barca way. I'm still not there, but it's a process," said 23-year-old Brugts.

"It's an interesting journey - to do it surrounded by the best players, some that have left and some that are still here.

"I'm super-grateful and I'm super-proud if I look at what's coming up from the younger teams. I'm very impressed with how good they are.

"The way Barcelona plays is something you have to learn when you are young. Whenever we need them, they are ready to play and understand the game."

#851. Ghana kick-start Afcon 2027 bid despite Ayew penalty miss

Jordan Ayew joined Championship side Sheffield United in September after spending two seasons with Leicester City

Ghana belatedly kick-started their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifying campaign with a 2-0 home win over Somalia.

The Black Stars had lost their opening two Group C matches against Ivory Coast and The Gambia, leading to the departure of coach Carlos Queiroz by mutual consent.

Ghana women's coach Kim Bjorkegren was placed in interim charge for this month's double-header against the Ocean Stars, with the West Africans in danger of missing a second successive edition of the Afcon finals.

The hosts were given a chance to take an early lead in Sekondi-Takoradi after Alidu Seidu was pulled down in the box, but Jordan Ayew's 14th-minute penalty was saved by Somalia goalkeeper Ibrahim Hussein.

Ghana did go ahead in first-half stoppage time when Mohammed Salisu headed Mohammed Kudus's deep corner back across goal and Jonas Adjetey nodded in from six yards out.

Felix Afena-Gyan doubled the Black Stars' advantage just after the hour mark when his shot from inside the box squirmed under Hussein and over the line.

The four-time continental champions remain six points behind group leaders Ivory Coast, who extended their 100% record by beating The Gambia 2-1 in Bouake.

Brighton midfielder Malick Yalcouye tucked in from seven yards out and Elye Wahi slotted home to double the Elephants' lead before Musa Barrow pulled one back for the visitors before the break.

Elsewhere on Thursday, there were wins for Cameroon, DR Congo and Senegal, who all remain on track to qualify for next year's tournament in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

The third round of qualifying fixtures continues on Friday with Egypt, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa in action among 12 fixtures.

Nicolas Jackson has 11 goals in 17 appearances for club and country this season

Nicolas Jackson set Senegal on their way to a 4-1 home win over Sudan in Group J, with Aston Villa team-mate Ibrahim Mbaye also on the scoresheet for Patrick Vieira's men in Dakar.

The Teranga Lions lead the standings on seven points, three ahead of Mozambique, who host Ethiopia on Friday.

Cameroon also remained unbeaten and moved on to seven points in Group G with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Namibia in Douala.

Meanwhile, Newcastle United striker Yoane Wissa opened the scoring as DR Congo continued their perfect start with a 3-1 triumph over Sierra Leone in Kinshasa.

The Leopards are on nine points at the top of Group E, five points ahead of Zimbabwe and Equatorial Guinea after those two sides drew 0-0.

Nigeria were handed a boost after Group L leaders Guinea-Bissau could only manage a 1-1 draw in their away tie against Madagascar in neutral Morocco.

The Super Eagles trail Guinea-Bissau by four points ahead of their home game against Tanzania on Friday (16:00 GMT).

Tanzania are assured of a place at Afcon 2027 as tournament co-hosts, with the other three sides battling for one qualification spot.

And Benin bolstered their bid to reach back-to-back finals with a 4-1 win over Central African Republic.

Gernot Rohr's Cheetahs lead Group F by three points from Burkina Faso, who entertain Mauritania on Friday.

In Group D, another section with just one spot available, Guinea moved level on points with table-toppers South Africa after seeing off Eritrea 2-1 in Conakry.

#850. Arsenal dig deep to earn WCL draw in face of Barcelona dominance

Arsenal continue to be a sharp thorn in the side of the European champions, Barcelona, and they dug deep to hold on to a draw at the Camp Nou on Thursday night. Frida Maanum put the Gunners ahead despite a hugely dominant performance from Barcelona, but Caroline Graham Hansen’s equaliser ensured the spoils would be shared.

Barcelona have been formidable when playing at the club’s main stadium, winning nine and drawing twice, against Chelsea in the semi-finals in 2023 and now Arsenal.

“Grit, resilience, discipline, clarity, communication, leadership, bravery – that’s a lot of words,” said Renée Slegers. “There’s a lot of really good things in this performance that we definitely want to build on.”

The last time these two teams met, Arsenal lifted the Champions League trophy at Barcelona’s expense after the most perfect defensive performance and a Stina Blackstenius goal in Lisbon in 2025. It was a far less perfect defensive performance this time but Arsenal showed the guts they have been missing at times this season, against the team that retook their crown last season, and showed they can play ugly when needed.

There was one change to the team that earned a 2-1 win against Liverpool on Sunday, but it was a significant one. Olivia Smith was replaced by Maanum and the Norwegian slotted into the No 10 role with Alessia Russo, who has scored 12 goals in nine games for club and country, moving into the centre-forward position.

It was the England forward’s play on the left that set up the shock first-half goal that temporarily silenced the crowd. She beat two and worked the ball to Maanum. Barcelona got the ball away but Russo was there again and delivered a perfect cross across the face of goal for Caitlin Foord. The Australian forced a close-range save from Cata Coll only for Maanum to power in the loose ball.

The pocket of travelling fans behind plexiglass in the upper tier were jubilant. About 1,000 had travelled despite the late switch of the match to Thursday due to a 24-hour general strike in Spain on Wednesday.

The goal came decidedly against the run of play but Barcelona struggled to capitalise on their first-half dominance. Ewa Pajor and Graham Hansen were particularly threatening as Barcelona targeted Arsenal’s left, made up of the less experienced Taylor Hinds and Lisa Baum.

The scoreline at the break was a little unfathomable based on the run of play and the domestic fortunes of both sides. While Arsenal languish in sixth in the WSL, 12 points behind the league leaders, Manchester City, Barcelona have won nine of their 10 games in Liga F, having scored 41 goals and built a five-point lead over their nearest rivals, Real Madrid.

Arsenal’s gameplan felt familiar. It was as if they had studied the blueprint religiously followed by teams that have sat back in a low block and frustrated them week-in, week-out in the WSL this season.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Aitana Bonmatí, the three-time Ballon d’Or winner, was surprisingly relegated to the bench but her arrival shortly before the hour elevated Barcelona’s threat, causing Arsenal’s defending to look even more calamitous at times, and lifted the mood in a frustrated stadium.

Three minutes after her arrival they were level. Esmee Brugts found an unmarked Graham Hansen on the right and she cut inside and swept in past Misa Rodríguez.

It was no surprise that Baum and Hinds, who had been run ragged, were removed soon after, with former Barcelona player Ona Batlle and Smith, Arsenal’s record signing, replacing them.

Arsenal were better after the goal and the changes, occasionally breaking free of their prison of a final third. At the end they were clinging on, but cling on they did.

“If we were to do it again, we’d try to stay on the ball for longer and play our game even more,” said Slegers. “Definitely there were moments in the first half and in the second half where we were really, really dangerous and created big chances, open chances. I’m just really pleased with the way we played the game tonight because it’s a very different game to what we usually play and that we can do it this way is a big boost for us as a team and that’s what we’re going to take with us going forward.”

#849. Owono undecided over future following De Miguel death

Owono has 47 caps for Equatorial Guinea but was not called up during the most recent international window

FC Andorra manager Carles Manso says goalkeeper Jesus Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

Owono was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during a Spanish second division match on 2 November, with the Tenerife forward passing away the following day in hospital.

Manso said the goalkeeper, 25, is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return.

"What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to âhim," Manso said.

"We will âgive him space so that he feels completely free to make âany â decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.

"When he feels it is appropriate and when âhe feels genuinely ready to take a âdecision â like that [he will do so]."

Andorra released a statement on behalf of Owono on 4 November, with the Equatorial Guinea keeper saying he was experiencing "the most difficult days of my life".

He added: "I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."

On Thursday, De Miguel's family released a statement via the Spanish Footballers' Association thanking those who had contributed to a crowdfunding page which has surpassed Â£170,000.

Fran Sol, a forward for Spanish third-tier side Hercules, set up the campaign with all proceeds going to relatives of De Miguel.

"We would like to express our heartfelt thanks for all the expressions of affection and support we have received," De Miguel's family said.

"We have been deeply moved to see so many of you rally behind this initiative."

Andorra will return to action for the first time since the forward's death on Saturday when they face Almeria in the Spanish second division.

#847. Young duo at heart of Nations League's meanest defence

Northern Ireland play Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday before travelling to Budapest to face Hungary on Tuesday

Across his two spells as Northern Ireland boss, Michael O'Neill has been blessed with no shortage of centre-back talent.

Jonny Evans, Aaron Hughes, Gareth McAuley and Craig Cathcart were mainstays of his first stint in charge - so much so that, in some of the biggest games of O'Neill's managerial career at Euro 2016, the quartet all started across a flat back-four.

Since returning to the job four years ago, O'Neill has switched to three at the back, with Sunderland duo Trai Hume and Dan Ballard providing an injection of Premier League quality in what remains a side largely drawn from the Championship and League One.

But with Hume, something of a Swiss army knife in the squad, covering the injured Conor Bradley on the right flank and even starting in centre midfield against Ukraine last month, and Ballard presently nursing an injured hamstring, change has been required through this Nations League campaign.

Despite those forced alterations in defence, the side go into their concluding Group B2 fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary top of their pool and the only side at any level of the competition yet to concede a goal.

At the heart of their defensive efforts have been Ruairi McConville and Tom Atcheson, two young centre-backs already described by their international manager as having "no ceiling".

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

At 21-years-old, Norwich City's McConville is the more senior of the pair.

Having been given his debut off the bench at home to Belarus two years ago this week, among the former Brighton man's early international assignments was trying to keep a rampant Alexander Isak in check during a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

In the short time since he has looked an increasingly commanding figure, leading this Nations League group in clearances made with both head and boot.

"It would be unbelievable to keep that record for these last two games and go the whole of the campaign," he said of what is Northern Ireland's longest run without conceding a goal since 2017.

McConville notes that the streak is a team effort and product of collective work-rate, rather than just the defensive three alone.

"We're a team that works hard, a team that doesn't want to give anything up.

"We're confident in ourselves and we know that we're a good side."

It is McConville who has taken on the Ballard role in the middle of the defence for the past three games, with Atcheson on the right and Oxford United's Ciaron Brown, himself superb through the campaign so far, playing from the left.

On the developing understanding between an emerging unit, McConville added: "We're enjoying playing together.

"It's still early days together and we have to keep taking it game by game and doing what the gaffer tells us and the work on the training pitch.

"We don't have much time together when we're here [in international camp] so it's important to do all we can."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Atcheson's comfort on the ball has been an asset across his six caps

After 16 caps, McConville is a relative veteran compared to Atcheson, who made his international bow in a friendly against Wales in March at a time when he had only four senior club starts to his name at Blackburn Rovers.

The most recent of those had come under O'Neill, then in a short stint as caretaker manager at the Championship club.

Clearly impressed by what he saw from the now 20-year-old at Ewood Park, Atcheson made his first Northern Ireland start against Guinea in June, a game in which he scored the winner with a fabulous flick before later being shown a red card.

Some 428 minutes into his international career, Atcheson is still to experience what it feels like to concede a goal.

The England-born defender feels Ballard "is definitely a big miss" to the side, but believes the squad's understanding of O'Neill's desired system is an asset to those who have starred during the Sunderland man's latest absence.

"I feel like everyone knows what they need to do, everyone knows their job, the details of the formation we play and system," he said.

"That's so key and I think that's why we're so solid defensively.

"It's a team thing, we're set up right, we're very on it all the time and everyone gives their all."

#846. SFA in talks with Boston officials over biennial friendly match

The Tartan Army made a big impression on the city of Boston during the World Cup

BBC Scotland has learned that the SFA is in active discussions aimed at a biennial friendly match being held in Boston.

Scotland played two World Cup matches in the US city during the summer and now the governing body and the state of Massachusetts are in talks aimed at building the bonds made between locals and the Tartan Army, through football.

More discussions are due to take place between the SFA and a delegation of state senators ahead of Scotland's Nations League match against North Macedonia at Hampden on Friday.

It has not yet been decided who will play in the game but BBC Scotland understands it will involve the Scoland national team.

US state senator Paul Feeney has been in the UK this week for talks around energy, but wanted to visit Scotland to build on the bonds made between the Tartan Army and those who partied with them for two weeks in June.

The state of Massachusetts has also passed a bill aimed at strengthening ties with Scotland after an estimated 25,000 fans partied in Boston and surrounding areas.

"We felt that this summer was more than just a football match, more than just, you know, 90 minutes at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough," Feeney said.

"It was a couple of weeks of these relationships being held, and you don't see that often. And I'm glad we got to experience it. And, frankly, we don't want that to end."

He added: "One of the things that we've been active on in Massachusetts today is to kind of take the lessons that we've learned, put together the best practices, and say, ok, we understand that we can't have a World Cup every year, but where we have such a strong connection with people in Scotland, could we do some sort of invitational tournament?

"To have that cultural exchange to kind of prop up economic development, and more than that, just to come together, have a few drinks, and enjoy each other's company."

Scotland fans placed cones on several Boston statues during their time in the city

Feeney said the Massachusetts Senate voted unanimously to support the concept.

"We're trying to work that through the legislature, get it to the finish," he said.

Talks aimed at organising a regular fixture are at an early stage but the SFA is already in advanced negotiations with businesses in Massachusetts about investment in the Scottish game.

"The Tartan Army invaded Massachusetts and I have to say they lit a spark that set off fireworks," Massachusetts Senate president Karen Spilka told BBC Scotland.

"They were sorely missed by so many people when they left.

"I think that by making the effort to come here and meet people and talk about tourism and economic development, we can start talking about things like Tartan Day and maybe having other events going on."

#845. Fitness, Fernandes and a back four: how next head coach can reignite Manchester United | Will Unwin

Michael Carrick’s replacement must find solutions on the pitch and pressure the hierarchy to accept a share of blame

One of the final images of Michael Carrick’s time in charge will be of him standing in the rain on the Old Trafford touchline watching his side succumb to Bournemouth, while his sullen captain sat unused on the bench. Bruno Fernandes was dropped after calling out his head coach’s tactics, although Carrick said it was for football reasons. It was the second combustible television interview in as many Champions League games after Lisandro Martínez pointed the finger at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, for failing to provide a squad suitable for fighting on all fronts.

Fernandes was soon back in the fold, and Martínez apologised for his outburst, but it is clear internal discipline is an issue and will be central to getting the team back on track. United will always draw more attention than almost any other club in the world and creating a circus around a failing team merely complicates matters when there are already enough problems to sort out on the pitch. The players need to harness their anger to ensure they create headlines for performances, not interviews.

One player Jason Wilcox could claim as a recruitment success was Senne Lammens but the goalkeeper’s form has joined that of his teammates in the gutter. The Belgian endured a horror show for Bournemouth’s third goal when he rushed out of his area, and he made two errors in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. Leny Yoro was another to make a terrible mistake against Bournemouth, while Diogo Dalot’s efforts as a makeshift left-back can be categorised as somewhere between woeful and inept. No team in Europe’s top five leagues have conceded more than United’s 30 in all competitions, which is clearly a worry.

Morale is at rock bottom but the chopping and changing in defence is creating more uncertainty. The new head coach should pick a back four and stick with it where possible. If Harry Maguire’s experience is deemed mandatory, he needs pace around him to make up for what he lacks. Luke Shaw’s absence has created a left-back tombola as Dalot, Ayden Heaven and Noussair Mazraoui have been placed there.

Benjamin Sesko’s injury has cost United a No 9 for most of the season and Joshua Zirkzee has rarely been trusted in the role. Matheus Cunha gave it a go as a false 9 and Bryan Mbeumo was tried as a more traditional centre-forward but without much success either. Cunha has become more productive in a deeper role behind the striker, cutting in from the left as he did at Wolves, but United require someone to be a classic No 9, someone who can occupy defenders and be serviced by deliveries from wide. Zirkzee, for his faults, has been a presence when used in recent weeks and scored against Aston Villa. If a new coach can rebuild his confidence, the Dutchman could provide a short-term solution. Alternatively, greater demands should be made of Marcus Rashford to play through the middle.

A mix-and-match of expletives were aimed at those above Carrick at recent home games. Wilcox has taken most of the individual criticism, but the ownership were told in no uncertain terms to sell up. The Glazers have been instrumental in driving the club downwards in recent years and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s investment and involvement in football operations have yielded little success.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Carrick was the face of the operation, as the new head coach will be, and he needs to put pressure on someone at the top to speak to the media to explain why the club is in such a mess because it is unfair to expect the coach to do so. United fans know the person in the dugout cannot take all the blame and someone else has to be publicly accountable.

Three central midfielders and a backup goalkeeper did not make for an inspiring summer when everyone knew United’s squad required improvement in numerous positions. Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba and Youri Tielemans started together against Bournemouth and offered no evidence for why so much was spent on them.

Whoever comes in needs to be clear about what is required, whether in the winter or summer windows, because the deficiencies in the squad mean United cannot compete on all fronts and are struggling to cope with the rigours of the Premier League. A new left-back and striker are a given, but there is plenty more work to be done.

Outrunning the opposition does not guarantee success but United have looked pedestrian on far too many occasions this season. This could explain the number of slow starts to games in recent times: in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid and Como they conceded in the first and second minute respectively, and were two down at home to Roma after 17 minutes last week. Worse still, Aston Villa, aided by errors, were two goals ahead within four minutes at Old Trafford, giving United a monumental task to turn things around. The players deserve credit for finding some fight to do so but need to make life easier for themselves because it does not take a genius to work out starting with a deficit is ill-advised. They will face a fiery atmosphere at Anfield, and that will be a fine place to show a shift in dynamic.

#843. English Soccer Star Jude Bellingham Reveals He Can’t Drive or Cook

Jude Bellingham, star of England’s men’s soccer team and Real Madrid, admitted his skills are limited to the pitch, and that he hasn’t yet learned how to drive or cook.

Jude Bellingham may be one of the greatest footballers of his generation.

But as it turns out, Team England’s star midfielder’s basic everyday skills—or lack thereof—help level the playing field, bringing him closer to us mere mortals.

“There’s loads of things I don’t know how to do,” Bellingham told British Vogue in an interview published Nov. 10. “I can’t cook, I can’t drive. I’m good at what I do, but everything else? Not that great. I rely on my friends, my family to help me do stuff—chef, cleaner, mum, whoever else. That’s where I’m at.”

In fact, he’s been so busy keeping his eye on the literal ball—and doing a really good job at it—he may have lost track of life’s other skills.

“I work hard every day and all day, and then when I get home,” the 23-year-old said, “I’ve probably neglected learning how to do some of the more basic things.”

In his defense, not only is learning those life skills par for the course for many early twenty-somethings, but Bellingham’s daytime job also takes up a lot of his time.

“I feel mature in a football context because I’ve played nearly 400 games,” he reflected. “But in a life context I don’t feel that mature now, to be honest.”

But, as he noted, “There’ll be a time and a place for that, I’m sure.”

In the meantime, he’s focused on his skills on the pitch, where Bellingham’s natural talents already having brough him to the World Cup twice, in 2022 and 2026. And in their most recent outing, England finished third—the country’s best result since 1966.

“The World Cup, for me, was probably the best experience I’ve had in my life, full stop,” the Real Madrid player said. “While I was in it, I really made the conscious decision to enjoy this.”

After all, “It doesn’t come around very often,” he added. “It’s rare.”

And while Bellingham’s World Cup performance won him fans around the world—as did his endearing bromance with former Borussia Dortmund teammate and Norway’s star Erling Haaland—nowhere was more grateful for his performance than England.

As he noted, “I’ve seen a lot of people say, ‘I don’t think I’ve ever had a night when I was so happy and so proud to be English.’”

For a look back at the many celebrities who tuned in live to see Bellingham’s athletic prowess shine on the pitch, read on.

#842. England's Blues brothers - how the Bellinghams helped save Birmingham

Jude Bellingham shared an old photo of him and brother Jobe after England's squad announcement last week

It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

While Jude, 23, is establishing himself as a footballing great at European greats Real Madrid following a spell at Borussia Dortmund, Jobe, 21, is continuing his football education at his brother's former club in Germany after two seasons with Sunderland.

The Stourbridge-born midfielders have moved on with their careers.

Their memories, however, live on at St Andrew's, such was the impact the boyhood Birmingham fans made in the Championship.

On match days supporters stop and pose for photographs in front of Jude's mural outside the ground. Fans still turn up to matches wearing Bellingham shirts.

"They both had a real connection with fans," Craig Courtney, from the Tilton Talk fan podcast, told BBC Sport. "Fans loved the fact they both cared.

"They wore their hearts on their sleeves and helped Birmingham when we were fighting relegation. Even now, Jude and Jobe remember where it all started for them."

The brothers played 70 league and cup games between them for Birmingham after graduating from the academy.

They have never appeared together in a senior match, however, as Jude - who joined Birmingham aged eight - had left by the time Jobe broke into the first team in 2022.

The Bellinghams will become the first brothers to play for England for 19 years if Jobe wins his first cap and appears alongside Jude, a veteran of 60 appearances, in the Nations League game with Croatia at Wembley.

"It will be an incredibly proud moment for Birmingham City if that happens," said Courtney.

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

Listen: How Jude Bellingham became a global brand

Birmingham supporters have had little to cheer about recently.

It is 15 years since they last appeared in the Premier League, while the 2011 League Cup winners even dipped down to League One recently.

While fierce rivals Aston Villa were playing - and beating - Bayern Munich and Bologna in the Champions League two years ago, Birmingham were losing at Shrewsbury and drawing with Northampton Town.

After 15 games Birmingham sit top of the Championship and there are plans for a new 62,000-capacity stadium in time for 2030-31.

"As a club, we've been right down in the doldrums," added Courtney. "Now we're top of the table and having a new stadium built.

"There is an argument that none of this would have been possible without the fees received for Jude and Jobe."

A mural tribute to Jude Bellingham outside St Andrew's

Jude is the youngest player in Birmingham's history after making his debut aged 16 years and 38 days in 2019.

Clubs across Europe were pursuing him when he signed his first professional contact in 2020 after turning 17 - a deal both he and Birmingham knew would never be fulfilled.

His actions, however, ensured Birmingham would receive a significant transfer fee when he left, and soon afterwards he joined Dortmund for an initial fee of Â£20m during the Covid-19 pandemic.

When he joined Real in 2023, Birmingham received a reported sell-on fee of at least Â£10m., external

"We cannot possibly imagine, without Jude's decision [to sign a contract], where we would be as a club in a pandemic like this," then Birmingham chief executive Xuandong Ren told BBC WM after Jude joined Dortmund.

"He could easily have just looked after himself and not the club, but he chose the best possible way to look after the club."

Jobe became the second youngest player to play for Birmingham when he made his debut in January 2022 aged 16 years and 107 days.

"This was a lad, regardless of who his brother was or what he was achieving, who would do anything to write his own success story," former Birmingham striker Troy Deeney, who played in the game when Jobe made his debut, told the Sun., external

"Everything he has achieved on the pitch, too, has come with an instant comparison to his older brother.

"He never got that one moment to enjoy something without someone, somewhere saying: 'Yeah, but what about Jude?'

"That only added to how strong he was mentally, and anyone who suggests he is where he is because of his last name is talking rubbish."

Deeney added: "What impressed me more than anything he had done on the pitch was his attitude - a hell-bent determination to get to the top and the common sense to take all the right steps along the way."

Jobe played 26 games before Sunderland paid Â£3m for him in 2023, with Birmingham receiving a reported Â£4m sell-on fee when he moved to Dortmund two years later.

Although significantly less than the fees generated by his brother, it was nevertheless welcome revenue.

Jobe Bellingham was given his Birmingham City debut by manager Lee Bowyer in January 2022

Both Jude and Jobe have returned to St Andrew's since their transfers.

Jobe captained England Under-21s to a 2-0 win against the Republic of Ireland at his old ground last November.

Before that match U21s boss Lee Carsley, who managed Jude when he was England interim manager in 2024, praised the brothers for their work ethic and determination to be the best.

Carsley said: "I know how much they love the Blues still and how important the club is to them."

Jude, tipped to be a future England captain, was at St Andrew's in July watching his former club in a pre-season friendly against Barcelona. He even wore a Birmingham shirt while watching from the stands.

Jude wore a Birmingham City shirt when he returned to St Andrew's

When Jude joined Dortmund in 2020 Birmingham retired the 17-year-old's number 22 shirt after 44 appearances.

"That was a gesture of thanks for what Jude had done," said Courtney.

"It might be wishful thinking, but I really believe Jude has unfinished business at Birmingham. I can see a scenario before he retires where he gets an opportunity to wear the number 22 again."

Should the Bellingham brothers play together against Croatia, they will become the first siblings to appear for England since Gary and Phil Neville against Spain in a friendly at Old Trafford in 2007.

It will be an immensely proud moment for their parents, Mark and Denise.

"We've played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life," Jude, a Champions League and La Liga winner with Real Madrid, wrote on social media, external in 2024.

"That would mean more than any of the trophies. Nothing would even get close to that... nothing."

BBC reporter John Watson has been finding out why Bellingham is proving so popular with football fans across the world

#841. Harry Kane spot on to seal England win over Croatia on his record-breaking night

It was an historic occasion for Harry Kane, the one when he made his 126th England appearance and overtook Peter Shilton as the nation’s most capped men’s player. And for much of the night, it felt as though the desire to celebrate him, certainly beforehand, was the main thing. The actual football in this Nations League group game felt like a sideshow.

England had demolished Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka last month; it was Croatia’s heaviest defeat. It was a different story here. England lacked cut and thrust. There was a flatness to the Wembley atmosphere. Croatia were never likely to be humbled again and they sensed redemption when Petar Sucic capitalised upon a defensive aberration from Jarell Quansah to equalise for 1-1 just before the hour.

It was at that point that Kane got a hold of the script. It was supposed to be his night during the 90 minutes, wasn’t it? There was a tussle on an England corner inside the Croatia area, Quansah feeling Ivan Smolcic tug at his shirt and when he went down, it felt as though the video assistant would be interested. He was, deciding that it added up to a penalty – and not that Quansah went to ground too easily.

It was over to Kane from the spot. There was the familiar stutter and the conversion was clipped up the middle, narrowly avoiding the trailing leg of the goalkeeper, Dominik Livakovic. It was Kane’s 92nd England goal; his 27th successful penalty.

Croatia fought until the end and they had a clutch of late chances, none better than when Nikola Vlasic took a touch and shot just wide in the 82nd minute. England were good value for the result. They are guaranteed a place in the quarter-finals of this competition in March and will go to Madrid to play Spain on Sunday with a shot at winning the group. They would have to beat the world champions to do that. And, really, play better than this.

Kane had walked out for kick-off with his four children and there was a lot for him – and them – to take in before a ball was kicked. First of all, there was the giant tifo behind one of the goals, which acclaimed Kane as “England’s finest”. Then, after he had hoisted aloft his Ballon d’Or trophy, there were presentations from Shilton, Luka Modric and Prince William. The gifts they bore, respectively, were a small trinket, a replica of the first football brought to Croatia in 1880 and a commemorative, framed Kane shirt.

It was quickfire. Rarely has so much been handed out so swiftly. Somewhat inevitably, there was a hangover when the game got under way. Was the show not already over? The Wembley crowded slumbered. Thomas Tuchel always wants intensity at the outset. It was not there.

Kane was involved in the breakthrough goal midway through the first-half, floating a lovely diagonal out to Jude Bellingham on the right-hand side of the Croatia area. Bellingham volleyed over first-time and what followed was a personal disaster for Josko Gvardiol. He got his feet into a tangle and allowed the ball to get to Morgan Rogers, who reached back and slashed it down and in from close-range.

Tuchel’s most eye-catching selection was to start Trent Alexander-Arnold over Ben White at right-back and the Real Madrid player got into advanced positions. He played some good balls. He wanted to quicken the collective pulse. As did Bellingham with those surges. It was all rather room temperature in the first half; England in control but not an awful lot happening.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Kane dropped deep. He wanted to spark England’s moves. He even took throw-ins. Rogers, who Tuchel played on the right wing, had the license to get into central attacking areas. Alexander-Arnold pushed high; sometimes as far as the centre-forward position.

Kane went close at the start of the second-half, seeing a close-range shot blocked and Bellingham did not get hold of a drive after Anthony Gordon had tried to buy a penalty with an obvious dive.

England were sleepwalking. It felt as though complacency set in. Elliot Anderson played a couple of loose passes. Lewis Hall needed to win a one-versus-one against Igor Matanovic, conceding a corner. From it, England got their wake-up call. Gvardiol challenged for the high ball and when it broke, Quansah tried to head back for Jordan Pickford; a high-risk move. He did not see Sucic, who stretched out a leg to touch home.

Enter Kane. The closing stages were notable for the booing of White when he came on to replace Alexander-Arnold and Croatia threatening a second equaliser. Quansah redeemed himself with a saving tackle on the substitute, Ante Budimir. At the other end, James Garner, on as a substitute, had the ball in the net only for Bellingham to be flagged offside. For England, it is on to the showdown with Spain.

#839. Aspyn Ovard Reveals 10-Year Secret Behind Parker Ferris Breakup

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star Aspyn Ovard shared the decade-long secret that led to her divorce from Parker Ferris on the show’s premiere: "It was literally earth-shattering."

Aspyn Ovard is sharing her truth about the end of her marriage to Parker Ferris.

Two years after their divorce, the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star revealed the infamous “10-year secret” fans have long awaited to learn: the real reason behind her breakup from Ferris.

“Publicly, I'd never shared why we got divorced,” Ovard said on the Nov. 12 premiere of the first season of the Hulu series. “When Parker and I were getting married, we were definitely—I thought, actually—we were on the same page about where we stood with drinking and smoking and things like that.”

While the YouTuber—who shares daughters Cove, 7, Lola, 5, and Elle, 2, with her ex—assumed she and Ferris both abstained from alcohol, she learned her then-husband wasn’t being truthful.

“My dad struggled with alcoholism, so the only version of him that I knew was some level of intoxicated,” Ovard recalled. “Whenever he would come home, and just the sound of his work boots, just like a dark cloud, over the house.”

“Finding out that Parker had been drinking behind my back for years, it was literally earth-shattering,” she continued, nodding in agreement when a producer asked if that was the big secret. “He went through so much to hide it from me, and the fact that my husband, who was supposed to be the safest person, would do that to me.”

The 30-year-old became emotional as she shared how learning of Ferris' hidden behavior impacted her, while also revealing how the timing made the situation even more difficult.

As Ovard told the cameras, “For him to know what alcoholism did to my family, to find all of this out two months after my dad died from alcoholism hurt so bad.”

In April 2024, the influencer shocked fans when she filed for divorce from Ferris—whom she married in 2015 when she was just 19 years old—the same day she announced the birth of their third baby.

Following the divorce, Ovard hinted on social media that she uncovered a decade-long secret that led to the dissolution of her marriage, which led to years of speculation and theories from fans about what went wrong.

And now that the truth is out there once and for all, the mom of three believes fans may be a little disappointed.

“People are going to be underwhelmed with what it is,” Ovard told E! News in an interview during the Mormon Wives’ junket. “But I think seeing him talk about it and then seeing me cry about it, maybe will give some perspective.”

“I’m very curious to see what people will say,” she added, “because I’ve seen some crazy theories and it’s just not that crazy of a thing.”

While time will tell how fans will react, the reality described going through that difficult time as “overwhelming” for her. That said, she’s not sure if she would do anything differently.

“I don’t know if I would handle things the same way if I could go back two years ago and talk about that all again,” Ovard admitted. “There’s no way to really navigate life when you’re just doing it all for the first time.”

Following her divorce from Cory Althoff, podcaster Bobbi Althoff is dating Tyler Hawkins, who plays a special role in Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"He styles me, that’s how he supports me,” she told E! News in May, adding that the basketball player, "picks out my outfits every day. He styles me every day for the show. It’s great."

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, also share 8-year-old twins Luca and Rue.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

Madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that."

But, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives."

Avery Woods and David Woods, parents to Ziggy and Stevie, are still feeling the love after a decade of marriage. As she simply put it, "my forever + always."

#838. Beyoncé Reveals New Details of “Very Small” Wedding to Jay-Z

Nearly 20 years after Beyoncé and Jay-Z tied the knot in a surprise 2008 ceremony, the “Crazy in Love” singer revealed ultra-rare details of their wedding.

After Jay-Z put a ring on it, Beyoncé had one must-have for their wedding.

The “Crazy in Love” singer recently shared ultra-rare insight into her and the “Empire State of Mind” rapper’s 2008 nuptials—including how her mother Tina Knowles ensured she loved the day like XO.

“My favorite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress,” the 45-year-old—mom to Blue Ivy, 14, as well as 9-year-old twins Rumi and Sir with Jay-Z—told i-D in an interview published Nov. 11. “It was gorgeously simple and made with her love.”

And the dress was the cherry, or love, on top of an otherwise perfect day.

“We have a very small wedding in our home,” she continued. “We told guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends.”

For Beyoncé, wearing a dress designed by her mother was a “very important” detail of her big day, adding, “more important than any designer dress.”

The “Break My Soul” singer and Jay-Z (real name Shawn Carter) are clearly feeling nostalgic for the journey they’ve taken both in love and their career.

After all, Jay-Z recently debuted his docuseries Jay-Z in 8 on HBO Max in September, which examines his life and career in eight episodes.

“I’m really excited,” Jay-Z told E! News of his family sharing in the milestone. “They know these things. We talk all the time. It'll be fascinating to see on a big screen and at times, I know it'll be, like, cringe.”

Although the rapper runs this town, he admitted he wasn’t feeling as bold when it came to getting vulnerable in front of his little ones.

“You know, when you put yourself out there like that,” he added, “you get embarrassed.”

Nevertheless, he emphasized, “It’s honest, and it's a beautiful piece. I'm very proud of it.”

And having both his career retrospective—his debut album Reasonable Doubt just celebrated its 30th anniversary in June—and milestone coincide felt especially kismet.

“It's just all aligned,” he said. “We didn't plan on it being part of a 30-year celebration. We were just, you know, creating a piece that we both believed in, and it just so happened it all lined up.”

#837. Survivor’s Brady Booker Reveals Shocking Fate of Severed Thumb

Survivor 51’s Brady Booker shared the bizarre fate of his injured thumb after he sliced off a "quarter” of the finger, which led to his surprising exit from the jury on the Nov. 11 episode.

Brady Booker may have lost much of his thumb on Survivor, but he left with a new accessory.

After the professional wrestler was eliminated from the competition series, he shocked viewers during the Nov. 11 episode by exiting the jury so he could receive medical attention for his severed finger. But now he’s sharing how the chopped off “quarter” of his thumb was able to make it home to the U.S. from Fiji—and revealing its unusual fate.

“It was sitting in a cooler,” Booker told Parade in a Nov. 11 interview, recalling what happened to his partial thumb in the days after he was voted off season 51 on Day 14. “And then when time arose, when people started asking questions about it, they asked me what I wanted to do with it.”

“There was kind of a talk that you can’t bring flesh across international waters; I guess I never really thought of that,” he continued. “As white as it was at the time, it kind of looked like a scallop still in the shell, so maybe we could pass as that.”

But instead of the 27-year-old’s severed thumb being reattached to his hand, it was turned into jewelry.

“They ended up putting it in some resin, putting it in a necklace,” Booker revealed. “When I got back, we put a clasp on it.”

The shocking reveal came after host Jeff Probst shared Booker decided he wasn’t going to be able to outwit, outplay and outlast on the island as a member of the jury, becoming the first player to leave the jury in show’s history.

“First, a little business,” Probst explained to the players on the Nov. 11 episode. “Last night, immediately following Tribal Council, Brady asked to go home to tend to his injured thumb. So, Brady is out of the game. He’s gone, and will not be a member of the jury.”

While Booker’s historic decision to leave Fiji was on Day 14 of the competition, his now-infamous injury occurred 10 days prior.

It was on the fourth day of the competition—which was chronicled on the Sept. 30 episode—when Booker accidentally cut off a “quarter” of his thumb while chopping firewood with a machete.

After acknowledging this “stupid” mistake, he detailed what went down while being looked at in the medical tent.

“I was just splitting some wood to get to the dry center with the axe," Booker explained to the doctor. “Had a little corner of my thumb, that little corner right there, and I just lopped it off. I truly feel like I can still compete and hopefully, we can do something.”

His wish was granted, with Booker expressing his relief that he was given the all-clear to continue after his thumb was wrapped.

“When Doc told me I can still be in this game, it was like a new life," he reflected. "Sure, it's still a little numb, but I can touch all the fingers. I can touch the far end. I can clap. I can grab. Sure, Brody, pain exists. But I'd rather feel pain than nothing at all.”

And while he was ultimately sent home—with a new necklace—he’s far from the only castaway to face a rocky journey on the island. Keep reading for a closer look at all of the players on Survivor 51…

Pitbull looks back on the stories behind some of his biggest hits, from “On the Floor” with Jennifer Lopez to “I Know You Want Me (Calle Ocho)” and “Give Me Everything” to “Timber” and “I Like It.” He shares how collaborations with artists such as Ne-Yo, Kesha, Lil Jon and Enrique Iglesias came together, why artists should fight for their song-publishing percentages, and how music can cross genres and bring people together. Plus, Mr. Worldwide reflects on the teacher who believed in him, and the schools he’s helping build to create opportunities for the next generation.

Pitbull: I said, “This is gonna be one big mother f–king record.” That’s what I kept saying, “This a big mother f–king. Oh, this is gonna be a big motherf–king.”

Leila Cobo: Last time you were here 10 years ago, you know that? Today we’re gonna talk a lot about music.

It was your first track that broke the top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100.

“I Know You Want Me” — very, very special record. But one, I wanna say thank you to Team Pitbull, and I got Robby Robb here, which is the person that sent me over the beat. It was, I believe, 75 Street Brazil was the name of the record. So he sends me over the beat. I’m driving around listening to the song, and I just listened to … I was on tour, and we were listening to Omega and El Cata. And then El Cata has a song, eh, I know you want me, you know I want ya. So he had that song, and I said, “OK, let me try it on,” and boom, I do it on there.

Now, Omega with the mambo and the whole nine is where we came up with little different things as far as how to get slick on the record. Here’s the most important part of this, especially for anybody here that’s trying to get in the music business: Make sure, numbers are numbers, you get me? Add, multiply, do add. I got that part. But when you’re talking percentages, that’s a different conversation. So make sure that you get your percentages on these records, ’cause that in turn is what’s gonna help you in the future. That’s gonna help your family. That’s called generational wealth. Triple G, generating to generate for generations.

El Cata, I, when I call him up, and I have a conversation with him, I say, “Cata, look, I’m going to give you a percentage of the song.” He says, “No, I don’t want that, bro. What I want is cash. Look, what I want is cash.” I say, “Look, I’m going to give you cash and I’m going to give you a percentage of the song.” He gets to Opa-locka and he’s telling me that I haven’t given him anything because this and that.

#831. Latin Grammys 2026: Full List of Winners (Updating)

Edgar Barrera arrives at the ceremony with 10 nominations, followed by CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, Jorge Drexler, Karol G and Rosalía, with seven each.

The Latin Grammys have arrived, with winners starting to be announced at 3 p.m. ET — hours before Thursday’s (Nov. 12) telecast — at the Premiere, a non-televised event where most of the trophies are handed out.

This year, Edgar Barrera tops the list of nominees with 10 nods. The acclaimed Mexican songwriter and producer appears in the general categories of record of the year, album of the year and song of the year — mostly for his work on projects by Karol G and Carín León — as well as songwriter of the year, an honor he has won for the past three consecutive years.

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, Jorge Drexler, Karol G and Rosalía follow with seven nominations each, while Silvana Estrada and Mon Laferte have six. All of them are vying for album of the year, alongside Anitta, Carín León, Milo J and Rawayana. Most also compete for song and record of the year.

Rosalía’s eclectic album LUX appears in fields including pop, alternative music, and Portuguese language music, in addition to album of the year. The Spanish superstar has already won the night’s top award twice before — in 2019 for El Mal Querer and in 2022 for Motomami — and she is once again widely considered a favorite.

At just 19 years old, Argentine singer and rapper Milo J arrives with five nominations, including in the three main categories, with a folk album. In addition, the album received a sixth nod, for best recording package.

Other contenders with multiple nominations include Arath Herce, with four; and BRUSES, Feid, Héctor Mazzarri, Jennifer Mosello and Eden Muñoz with three each. Artists such as Rauw Alejandro, Anitta, Bad Gyal, Beéle, Bizarrap, Ryan Castro, Daddy Yankee, Kany García, Joaquina, Juanes and Carín León, among others, received two nods.

Daddy Yankee is set to take the stage as the Latin Recording Academy’s 2026 Person of the Year, a day after he was celebrated at a traditional dinner-concert by his peers. The coveted Latin Grammy for best new artist will be contested by Delilah, Fabian, Loulu Gilberto, Arath Herce, Macario Martínez, Maye, Sofia Monroy, Kendall Peña, Dora Sanches, Aria Vega and Zeca Veloso.

The 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards will be broadcast live from Las Vegas starting at 8 p.m. ET on TelevisaUnivision platforms. The Premiere began at 3 p.m. ET on the official digital platforms of the Latin Recording Academy, including its Latin Grammys channels on YouTube, Facebook and X.

Below is the complete list of winners for the 2026 Latin Grammys, which we will be updating throughout the day. (The eligibility window was for recordings released June 1, 2025, through May 31, 2026).

#828. Ben Stiller Reveals Why He's More Protective of His Kids Than Ever

Ben Stiller reflected on his "protective" parenting style for his and his wife Christine Taylor's kids Ella and Quinn in an exclusive E! News interview at the Focker In-Law world premiere.

Ben Stiller isn't focking around when it comes to his kids.

The actor admitted that as his and wife Christine Taylor's kids Ella Stiller, 24, and Quinlin Stiller, 21, have gotten older, he's found himself following the path of his now-overbearing Focker In-Law character Greg Focker.

"I always was more of a Greg guy in terms of, I didn't have a lot of rules and stuff like that," Stiller exclusively told E! News at the movie's world premiere on Nov. 11. "But then, as you let them out into the world, they live their lives, you care about them, you see things coming at them, and you want to be protective.

Similar to Greg's own arc, however, he added, "You try to hold back, too."

Focker In-Law—premiering in theaters Nov. 25—follows Greg as his now-adult son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) brings home his girlfriend Olivia (Ariana Grande) for the first time. More than 25 years after Greg had to impress his now-wife Pam's retired CIA agent/veteran dad Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro) in Meet the Parents, the tables have turned.

"I understand the Jack Byrnes tendencies, which are similar, honestly, to the Greg [Focker] ones," Stiller posited, "which are to be protective. It's just different ways of expressing it."

After all, while Greg was competing with Olivia—life coach and former FBI hostage negotiator—to establish dominance while riding bikes, Jack strapped her for a polygraph test.

But when it came to working with Grande, Stiller was so into welcoming her to the Focker family.

"She just has amazing timing," he recalled. "She's really, really good. I'd seen her in Wicked, and I knew she was great at doing a very specific kind of character. In this movie, she really pulled something off in creating this person who you're wondering about."

"You're not necessarily rooting for her, but then you are rooting for her," he continued, "because she is a good person, but she's also kind of interesting, too. She gave it all these great colors and she was amazing."

Meanwhile, the Zoolander star admitted he can't quite relax when he reunited with De Niro—with whom he starred in 2000's Meet the Parents, 2004's Meet the Fockers and Little Fockers in 2010—once again.

"Over the years, we've gotten to know each other a little bit, but not that well," he admitted, but teased, "Enough that I'm still intimidated when I see him. I feel like that's always gonna be there. That's part of the dynamic."

But even blue steel wasn't strong enough to calm his nerves while working with the Oscar winner.

"It's always a little something because he's always Robert De Niro," Stiller emphasized. "He is a living legend for us actors."

Now, keep reading to see more of Stiller and Taylor's really, really, really ridiculously good-looking family moments.

Married since 2000, Ben Stiller and wife Christine Taylor broke up in 2017. However, they never filed for divorce. And after to quarantining together with their kids Ella and Quinlin during the pandemic, they reconciled for good.

Ella has often accompanied her father to events over the years, joining Stiller at the June 2023 Tribeca Film Festival debut of the short film Let Liv, which her mom also starred in. For the outing, the trio coordinated in different black outfits.

Previously, Ella served as her dad's plus-one at the 2022 Emmys, the 2018 premiere of Free Solo, the 2017 premiere of The Meyerowitz Stories and the opening night of the Broadway musical Groundhog Day.

In 2019, the duo went to the 2019 Golden Globes together to support Escape to Dannemora, the Showtime miniseries that earned Stiller a nomination for Outstanding Directing.

"I was very happy it went well," the Zoolander actor told E! News of working with Ella. "She showed me a lot of respect, which I appreciated because with a teenage daughter you want to be like, 'Don't be like how we are at home! Let's pretend we're actually nice to each other!' No, it was really a super positive experience for both of us."

In addition to her small role in Escape to Dannemora, Ella has also made appearances in Hubie Halloween and Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb.

As Stiller told E! in 2019, Ella "seems to have a desire to explore" an acting career.

Taylor also spoke about Ella's decision, telling Us Weekly in 2018 that she never "discouraged" her from following in her parents' footsteps.

"She came out of the womb with a mission, and I was never going to get in her way," The Brady Bunch Movie alum explained. "She is a very strong-minded, strong-willed young lady, and she loves it. Obviously she was born into the world, but I think living in New York City, she has been exposed to so many incredible things and shows and so … she has the bug. There's nothing you can do about it, but I did not encourage it."

Stiller previously revealed that Ella had a conversation with him about "not being there" during her childhood due to his career.

"She's pretty articulate about it, and sometimes it's stuff that I don't want to hear. It's hard to hear," he explained to Esquire. "Because it's me not being there in the ways that I saw my parents [actors Jerry Stiller and Anne Meara] not being there. I had always thought, 'Well, I won't do that.'"

While Stiller noted that it "didn't feel great" to hear Ella say that, he said it was "important to acknowledge" her feelings: "But then it's that thing that, like, I was trying to navigate my own desire to fulfill the hopes and dreams I had, too."

The Severance director went on to say that Ella and her brother Quinlin were never keeping notes on his absences due to work, they just wanted to spend quality time with their dad.

"What I've learned is that your kids are not keeping score on your career," he explained. "It would be solipsistic to think that my kids actually care about that. They just want a parent who's emotionally present and supportive of them. That's probably what they want more than for me to be going off and pushing the bounds of my creativity."

During an appearance on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, Stiller revealed Ella had turned him into a major Taylor Swift fan after she made him listen to the singer while he was teaching her how to drive.

"What really helped her was if we just played her favorite artist on the iPhone, and we just played Taylor Swift," he explained. "I was a fan, but I think now I'm a total Swiftie."

Swift's music "would calm her, and it would calm me," Stiller shared before going on to prove just how big of a fan he's become. "We got into the later stuff—Folklore, Evermore. 'Cardigan,' 'Betty' and 'August' all being about the same love triangle but from different points of view. And the characters are named after Ryan Reynolds' and Blake Lively's kids. And then the 'All Too Well' 10-minute Taylor's version from the vault."

After filming Tropic Thunder with Stiller in 2007, Taylor chose to take a break from acting to focus on raising their kids.

"It never felt like a big decision for me," she shared during an appearance on The Morning Call in 2010. "When I had Ella, my whole world changed. I couldn't believe how much love I had for this little creature. I wanted to be a part of it all. I didn't want to miss anything, and with Ben working as much as he does, I felt it was important for one of us to be the stability in the family."

Stiller told Parade in 2016 that he felt "very fortunate" that Taylor made that decision.

Stiller and Taylor decided to adopt a plant-based lifestyle more than a decade ago and inspired their kids to do the same.

"Ben and I make these green drinks in the morning and they look at us like it's from another planet," she told People in 2012. "I joke, 'Just join the party! Don't complain so much, just join us.'"

The Search Party actress went on to detail Ella and Quinlin's differing tastes, saying, "My daughter loves veggies but doesn't love fruit. My son loves fruit and doesn't love veggies."

Still, Taylor hasn't given up hope. "It's that thing where your parents aren't cool for a while and then suddenly they are," she explained. "We just kind of plant the seeds."

While Ella often attends events with her parents, Quinlin rarely makes public appearances. Though he did attend the Project A.L.S. Benefit in 2018 with his family.

"This is his first event. I think he's just having fun with it," Taylor told Us Weekly at the time. "Last year, our daughter came to the event for the first time and she encouraged him to come this year, and being able to make it fun and again the extended family that we've built and I think we've seen each other for 20 years and we've all watched our kids grow up."

Quinlin also attended the Project ALS 25th Anniversary Gala in 2023, just one of many passion projects the couple have shared with their kids.

"For them to come out on a school night," Taylor, who sits on the board of directors for the organization, noted to Us Weekly in 2018, "have a little fun, dress up, take some pictures, but then learn about an incredible organization, that's huge."

#825. Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King

Andy Robertson is one of two centurions for Scotland men

Andy Robertson says it gives him "goosebumps" any time he thinks about it.

Friday at Hampden, North Macedonia the visitors, a 102nd cap to be won and, when it is, he'll be level in the pantheon with Sir Kenny Dalglish, the football man he loves more than any other.

On Monday in St Gallen, Switzerland - all being well - Robertson will break the great man's record, a mark that has stood for 40 years.

The Tottenham left-back is sitting in the boardroom at Queen's Park in the shadow of Hampden with a phone in his hand and eyes fixed on his 19-year-old self coming off the bench in Warsaw on 5 March, 2014.

"Nervous, excited, living the dream, not knowing what road I was on," he smiles as he looks at the moment he takes his first touch in international football.

"As I was going on, Gordon [Strachan, Scotland manager] said to me, 'remember why you're here, play like you play at Dundee United, don't play safe'. The first ball, when it came to me, I just drove forward about 30, 40 yards.

"I had pretty much every emotion that day. My mum and dad were there. My brother. My aunt and uncle. My other uncle. There's a picture of me and my brother [Stephen] at the airport after the game. He had a big Poland hat on and a half-and-half scarf. He was well oiled by that point."

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

Robertson says he'd have laughed out loud had you told him then what lay ahead of him - two Premier Leagues, two League Cups, an FA Cup, a Champions League, a Super Cup, a Club World Cup, soon-to-be the most capped male Scottish players in history and, by a mile, the one with the most games as captain of the men's team.

"I've never actually been confident," he says, which is a surprise admission given everything he's done.

Maybe what he means is that he always had a quiet belief in his own ability but found that constantly questioning himself was who he was and who maybe who he still is.

"I've always doubted myself and that's always got the best out of me. I've always tried to prove people wrong and prove myself wrong. The one thing I didn't do was look too far ahead. I always just lived in the here and now and that's served me well."

In the room where he's talking there are a dozen normal chairs and away to the side, detached from the rest, is an elaborate seat. A high-backed, ornate, somewhat regal affair.

It looks fit for a king and, given the history Robertson's about to make, maybe he should plonk himself in it. And that brings us back to the man whose record he's about to match and surpass.

"There are normal seats but there's one throne and Kenny Dalglish should be sat on it," he says. "Friday night's not about me. Friday night's about the greatest player of all time in our country, and for me, that will always be Kenny.

You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career

"He's had this record for so long. He deserves it. If he played in a different era, he would probably have played a number of games that wouldn't have been able to be caught.

"Sometimes - not as a criticism - as a country we're maybe not good at recognising how good people we've got are. For me, he's the best player to ever play with Scotland and arguably Britain.

"We have to appreciate that man because I certainly do, my family certainly do and, I think on Friday, I'll have him at the front of my mind, the back of my mind and I'm not really bothered about myself."

It's a lovely thing, that. Robertson, about to draw level with Dalglish, is only thinking about Dalglish.

The depth of feeling comes tumbling out of him when he starts telling stories about what King Kenny means to his family and how he seemingly created a miracle by momentarily curing Robertson's beloved late grandfather's hearing.

"I always remember my agent talking to me about the first time he met Liverpool," Robertson says of a time when he was still with Hull but about to move to Anfield.

"He met the chief scout and sporting director and all of a sudden Kenny 'accidentally' walked into the room. It was 100% planned, I know it was planned.

'It means everything' - numbers behind Robertson's 100-cap Scotland career

You are Scotland boss Pocognoli - what would you do?

No excuses as Pocognoli seeks first Hampden victory

"One of the things right at the top of the list for me was the fact [by joining Liverpool] I got to meet Kenny in person and I've actually got to have a relationship with him and his family, because his family are special.

"My dad, in particular, has met people in football through me, but I've never seen him being starstruck by anyone apart from Kenny.

"I always remember, we'd just beaten Barcelona 4-0 [in May, 2019] to qualify for my second Champions League final. My grandad was at the game and I managed to grab Kenny afterwards. I says, 'Kenny, would you mind coming in to see my grandad and my uncle? They would love to see you'.

"Bear in mind his grandson's just qualified for another Champions League final and he basically barged me out of the way and shook Kenny's hand.

"My grandad had hearing aids. He couldn't really hear much of us but he heard everything Kenny said, so it did open a lot of questions in the family as to how bad the ear problem was with my grandad. He's no longer with us but to see how happy he wasâ¦ Kenny was his hero."

When Robertson moved to Liverpool for the hilariously small sum of Â£8m in 2017, his wife, Rachel, was expecting their first child. The Dalglishes, he says, helped so much that he could hardly ever repay them for their support and friendship.

On the pitch and off, the transfer to Liverpool as a 23-year-old was the greatest move he could have possibly made.

In reflective mood, on the cusp of Scottish football history, Robertson talks about his mother and father and his brother. "They're as proud of my brother as they are of me," he said. "The exact same, whatever achievements we have. But I think they're more proud of the men we've become. That was always most important for me.

"Anyone who knows me, my family, my friends, I always want them to like the person first, the footballer second. Anyone that only wants to know me as the footballer, then I don't let them get too close but if they want to know me as the person first and foremost, then they're the people that are really in my close circle.

"I've still got the same friends I went to nursery with at three years old. Three of my best friends."

Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson

Robertson hits 100 Scotland caps - but which other men make top 10?

Robertson says he often thinks about the game in Scotland and whether young kids today are getting the kind of opportunities he got. "We talk about that - my story, John McGinn's story, Ryan Christie's story," Robertson said.

"There'll be a hundred people going, 'I could have been that'. Football has a lot to do with ability and mentality, but also you need a little bit of luck as well.

"It's about trying to protect the 15, 16, 17-year-olds just now and we all have a duty to help with that. We always want the young players to come in and I just love their energy, I love how excited they are. Findlay Curtis just bounces about all the time.

"These are the kids that are going to bring the country forward. They're all sitting at the other end of the table playing games we don't even know about but it's great for us to sit back and go, 'OK, we're part of this squad, but when we leave, then hopefully Scotland will be in a good place."

To Friday, then. A record-equaller but, to Robertson, this is no nostalgia trip. This is a game Scotland desperately want - and need - to win.

He says they were a yard off it in all areas last time out against Slovenia. "Unacceptable," he recalled. "We didn't give our fans anything to shout about."

He departs with fighting words about the desire within the squad to make amends. Out the door, down the corridor and onwards into history. Seconds later, he returns. "Forgot my washbag," he laughed. "Bet Kenny didn't have one of these!"

Glasgow, Liverpool, Scotland - the ties that bind.
